How a Muslim actually prays

Times, washing, direction, and what happens inside one cycle.

The five times are set by the sun, so they shift daily and vary enormously by latitude. Fajr — from true dawn until sunrise. Ẓuhr — after the sun passes its zenith. ʿAṣr — late afternoon. Maghrib — just after sunset. ʿIshāʾ — once twilight has gone. Each obligatory prayer has a set number of cycles: two at Fajr, four at Ẓuhr, four at ʿAṣr, three at Maghrib, four at ʿIshāʾ.

Wuḍūʾ, the ablution, precedes prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, forearms to the elbows, wiping the head, then the feet to the ankles. It lapses with sleep and certain bodily functions and must then be repeated. Where water is unavailable, tayammum with clean earth substitutes.

The qiblah is the direction of the Kaʿbah in Mecca. Early Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem; the direction was changed during the Medinan period (2:144), and the reorientation is one of the most consequential single verses in Islamic history.

Inside one rakʿah — the unit a prayer is counted in:

  • Takbīr — hands raised, "Allāhu akbar." From this moment ordinary speech and action are suspended.
  • Qiyām — standing, reciting Sūrat al-Fātiḥah and then another passage of the Qur'an.
  • Rukūʿ — bowing from the waist, back level, glorifying God.
  • Iʿtidāl — returning upright.
  • Sujūd — full prostration, forehead and nose to the ground. Performed twice, with a brief sitting between.

The prayer closes seated with the tashahhud and the taslīm — turning the head right and then left with "peace be upon you and the mercy of God," addressed to those beside you and, in the classical understanding, to the recording angels.

Jumuʿah, Friday, replaces the midday prayer with a congregational sermon and two cycles. It is not a sabbath — there is no prohibition on work in Islam, and people return to their business afterwards.

The call. The adhān announces each prayer time; the iqāmah announces that the congregation is about to begin. In Muslim-majority cities the day is audibly divided into five parts, which is a thing you notice most sharply when you leave one.

What a Muslim life looks like across a year and a lifetime

The lunar calendar, the festivals, and the rites from birth to burial.

The year is lunar — twelve months of 29 or 30 days, about 354 days in total. Because it is not corrected against the solar year, it drifts roughly eleven days annually, so Ramadan moves through every season across a lifetime. A Muslim in Norway will fast a twenty-hour summer day and, some twenty years later, an eight-hour winter one.

Two festivals. ʿĪd al-Fiṭr ends Ramadan — a charitable payment (zakāt al-fiṭr) is due before the prayer so that the poor can also celebrate. ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā falls during Hajj and commemorates Ibrāhīm's willingness to sacrifice his son; an animal is slaughtered and the meat divided in thirds between the household, relatives, and the poor.

Also marked: Muḥarram, particularly ʿĀshūrāʾ, observed very differently by Sunnis (a recommended fast) and Shia (mourning for the killing of Ḥusayn at Karbala); Laylat al-Qadr in the last ten nights of Ramadan, "better than a thousand months" (97:3); and Mawlid, the Prophet's birthday, celebrated in much of the Muslim world and rejected as an innovation in some currents.

A life, in rites. The adhān is whispered into a newborn's ear, so the first words a Muslim hears are the ones they will hear five times a day. ʿAqīqah — a naming and sacrifice around the seventh day. Circumcision for boys. Nikāḥ — marriage as a contract, requiring the consent of both parties, witnesses, and a mahr paid by the groom to the bride and belonging to her alone.

Death is deliberately plain and fast. The body is washed, wrapped in simple white cloth, prayed over (ṣalāt al-janāzah, performed standing, without bowing or prostration) and buried — usually within a day, without a coffin in most traditions, lying on the right side facing Mecca. Embalming and display are avoided. Grave markers are kept modest, on the principle that the poorest and the wealthiest should be indistinguishable at the end.

Everyday texture. Bismillāh before eating, al-ḥamdu lillāh after, in shāʾ Allāh before any statement about the future — a grammatical habit of never claiming certainty about what has not happened. Dietary law (ḥalāl and ḥarām) excludes pork, blood, carrion and intoxicants, and requires a specific method of slaughter. Interest (ribā) is prohibited, which has produced an entire parallel field of Islamic finance.

Qadar — the article that caused the deepest split

If God decrees everything, in what sense do I choose?

The sixth article is the one Islamic theology has fought over hardest, and the dispute is the same one Christian and Jewish thinkers reached by other routes.

The Qadariyyah and the Muʿtazilah held that humans create their own acts. Otherwise, they argued, divine justice collapses — God cannot punish a person for an act He Himself produced. Reason can establish what is good, independently of revelation.

The Jabriyyah took the opposite extreme: human action is compelled outright, and apparent choice is illusion.

Al-Ashʿarī (d. 936), who began as a Muʿtazilite and broke with them, proposed the position most Sunnis hold: the doctrine of kasb, "acquisition." God creates the act; the human being acquires it, and that acquisition is what responsibility attaches to. Critics on both sides have called this a name for the problem rather than a solution — a charge Ashʿarites have been answering for a thousand years.

The Māturīdī school, dominant alongside Ḥanafī law across South and Central Asia, allows reason a larger role than Ashʿarism does while stopping short of the Muʿtazilite position.

The parallel arguments in Christian and philosophical form — Molinism, open theism, compatibilism — are set out in Theology. No tradition has produced a resolution that satisfies the other side.

Sunni and Shia — what the division is actually about

A question of legitimate authority that became a theological tradition.

The original dispute, in 632 CE, was over who should lead the community after the Prophet's death. Sunnis held that the community selects its leader, and accepted the first four caliphs. Shia held that leadership belonged to ʿAli, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, and to his descendants by divine designation.

A succession question became a theological one: Shia Islam developed the doctrine of the Imamate, with the Imams as divinely guided interpreters. Twelver Shia — the large majority of Shia, dominant in Iran and Iraq — hold that the twelfth Imam is in occultation and will return.

The creed is structured differently, not just populated differently. Twelver Shia organise belief as five uṣūl al-dīn, roots of religion: Tawḥīd (divine oneness), ʿAdl (divine justice), Nubuwwah (prophethood), Imāmah (the imamate), and Maʿād (the return and judgement). Angels and books are folded into the first and third rather than listed separately; ʿAdl is raised to a root of its own, reflecting the Shia inheritance of Muʿtazilite reasoning about divine justice; and Imāmah has no Sunni counterpart at all.

Practice is organised as ten furūʿ al-dīn, branches: prayer, fasting, hajj, zakāh, khums (a further fifth of certain surplus, with no Sunni equivalent), jihād, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, tawallā (loyalty to the family of the Prophet) and tabarrā (dissociation from their enemies). The five pillars are all present — they are simply not the organising frame.

Proportions: roughly 85–90% Sunni, 10–15% Shia, with the precise split genuinely uncertain because several relevant states do not collect the data.

Legal schools. Sunni jurisprudence runs through four surviving madhhabs — Ḥanafī, Mālikī, Shāfiʿī, Ḥanbalī — which differ on method and on many rulings while recognising each other as valid. Twelver Shia follow the Jaʿfarī school. Sufism, the mystical dimension, cuts across all of these and is not a separate sect.

Qur'an, Hadith, and how a ruling is built

Four sources, in strict order of authority.

Qur'an — the primary source. Compiled into a single standard text under the caliph ʿUthmān within about two decades of the Prophet's death.

Sunnah — the Prophet's practice, transmitted as hadith. Each report carries an isnād, a named chain of transmitters, and a whole science exists to grade those chains: ṣaḥīḥ (sound), ḥasan (good), ḍaʿīf (weak), mawḍūʿ (fabricated). The major Sunni collections are those of al-Bukhārī and Muslim; Shia collections include al-Kāfī.

Ijmāʿ — scholarly consensus. Qiyās — reasoning by analogy to new cases.

The result is a jurisprudence that is explicitly probabilistic in much of its output. Classical jurists routinely ended rulings with wa-Allāhu aʿlam — and God knows best — which is a statement about the limits of human interpretation, not a rhetorical flourish.

Sharīʿah is the whole path — worship, ethics, family, commerce — derived through fiqh, the human discipline of interpretation. The distinction between the divine law and the fallible jurisprudence that reads it is central, and is frequently collapsed by outside commentary and by some inside it.

Hinduism: A Family of Traditions, Not a Church

Rigveda c. 1500 BCE · Upanishads c. 800–200 BCE · Gita c. 200 BCE–200 CE

No founder, no single scripture, no central authority, and no requirement that its schools agree with one another — including about whether God exists.

Shared vocabulary

Dharma — the right ordering of things, and your particular duty within it. Karma — action and its consequence, operating as a moral law rather than a punishment. Saṃsāra — the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Mokṣa — release from that cycle, the highest aim.

Ātman is the self; Brahman is ultimate reality. The relationship between the two is the great question, and the schools answer it differently — which is precisely why "Hinduism" is a family term.

Three answers to one question

Advaita (Śaṅkara, 8th c.) — non-dualism. Ātman is Brahman; the appearance of separateness is māyā. Liberation is recognition, not achievement.

Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja, 11th–12th c.) — qualified non-dualism. Selves are real and distinct, yet exist as the body of God. Devotion is the path.

Dvaita (Madhva, 13th c.) — dualism. God and souls are permanently distinct; grace is required.

All three read the same Upanishads with the same care and reach incompatible conclusions. The tradition holds them simultaneously.

The texts, in two categories

Śruti — heard; smṛti — remembered.

Śruti ("that which is heard") is regarded as eternal and unauthored: the four Vedas, ending in the Upanishads. The Rigveda was transmitted orally with such precision — using multiple redundant recitation patterns as error-checking — that it survived over a millennium before being written down.

Smṛti ("that which is remembered") carries human authorship: the Mahābhārata (which contains the Bhagavad Gītā), the Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras.

In practice the Gītā — Krishna's counsel to Arjuna on a battlefield about acting without attachment to results — is the most widely read text of all, despite sitting in the second category.

Four paths, and the devotional streams

Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism — and why the "330 million gods" figure misleads.

Four yogas — jñāna (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (selfless action) and rāja (meditative discipline). Different temperaments, the same destination.

Major streams — Vaishnavism (Vishnu and his avatars, including Rama and Krishna), Shaivism (Shiva), Shaktism (the Goddess), and Smartism (which treats several deities as equivalent approaches to one reality).

On the many gods. The frequently quoted "330 million deities" rests on a reading of Sanskrit koṭi, which means both "crore" and "kind" or "category." More importantly, most Hindu theology treats the devas as aspects or manifestations of a single ultimate reality — the Rigveda itself says "truth is one; the wise call it by many names" (1.164.46). Calling Hinduism straightforwardly polytheistic is a category error that its own philosophers rejected long ago.

Belief, practice, prayer, and a life

Four aims, four stages, sixteen rites — and a household shrine.

What is believed. There is no creed, no council and no authority able to define one — so the shared content is a framework rather than a set of propositions. Dharma, right conduct appropriate to your situation. Karma, action and its consequence, operating as impersonal law. Saṃsāra, the cycle of rebirth. Mokṣa, release from it. Ātman and Brahman, self and ultimate reality — whose relationship the schools answer incompatibly, as set out above.

Two structures organise a Hindu life more concretely than any doctrine. The four puruṣārthas, legitimate aims of human life: dharma (duty), artha (prosperity), kāma (pleasure and love) and mokṣa (liberation). Note that wealth and pleasure are on the list — this is not a tradition that treats worldly life as a distraction to be endured.

The four āśramas, stages of life: brahmacarya, the student; gṛhastha, the householder, who supports everyone else and is treated in the texts as the foundation of society; vānaprastha, gradual withdrawal; and sannyāsa, renunciation. A full life is understood as moving through all four in order, and the modern reality is that most people spend it in the second.

How it is practised. Largely at home. Most Hindu households keep a shrine, and pūjā — the daily offering — is performed there rather than in a temple: the mūrti, the image of the deity, is treated as an honoured guest and is woken, bathed, dressed, offered flowers, incense, light and food. The food, once offered, becomes prasād and is eaten by the family.

Temple worship works differently. The purpose is darśana — seeing and being seen by the deity — rather than congregational service. There is no set weekly gathering and no obligation to attend, which is why the Christian and Muslim question "when do you go?" does not translate.

How it prays. Not primarily by petition. Japa is the repetition of a mantra, counted on a mālā of 108 beads. The Gāyatrī mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10), a request for illumination of the intellect, is recited at dawn and dusk as part of sandhyāvandanam. Ārtī — the circling of a lamp before the image, accompanied by singing — closes most acts of worship, in homes and temples alike. Bhajan and kīrtan are devotional singing, often for hours and often collective.

Alongside all of this runs a contemplative track: the meditative discipline of rāja yoga, the eight limbs codified by Patañjali, of which the physical postures now exported worldwide are a single limb.

What a life looks like. Marked by saṃskāras, rites of refinement, traditionally sixteen: rites before and at birth, the first feeding of solid food, the first haircut, upanayana — the sacred thread, marking the start of formal study — vivāha, marriage, and antyeṣṭi, the last rite. Cremation is near-universal, with the ashes committed to a river; the eldest son traditionally lights the pyre.

The year is dense with festivals, and they vary sharply by region and by which deity a family follows. Dīwālī, lights and the new year in much of India. Holī, colour and the licensed collapse of social distinction for a day. Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā, nine nights for the Goddess. Janmāṣṭamī, Krishna's birth. Mahā Śivarātri, a night vigil for Shiva. Pilgrimage (tīrtha-yātrā) to Varanasi, Rameshwaram, Kedarnath and the rest is a lifelong aspiration rather than an obligation; the Kumbh Mela is the largest human gathering on earth.

Vegetarianism is common but not universal, and beef is avoided very widely. Fasting is frequent, partial and tied to particular days of the week associated with particular deities rather than to a single season.

Buddhism: Diagnosis Before Doctrine

Siddhārtha Gautama, c. 5th century BCE, northern India

The Buddha declined to answer whether the universe is eternal or whether there is a creator. He said those questions do not help, and offered a diagnosis and a treatment instead.

The Four Noble Truths
  • Dukkha. Existence involves unsatisfactoriness — not merely pain, but the instability of everything we try to hold.
  • Samudaya. Its origin is craving — taṇhā, thirst — including the craving for existence itself.
  • Nirodha. Cessation is possible. This is the claim everything else rests on.
  • Magga. There is a path: the Eightfold Path, grouped as ethical conduct, mental discipline and wisdom.

The structure is deliberately medical — symptom, cause, prognosis, prescription — and the Buddha compared metaphysical speculation to a man shot with an arrow who refuses treatment until he knows who fired it.

The three marks

Anicca — impermanence. Nothing persists unchanged, at any scale.

Dukkha — the unsatisfactoriness that follows from trying to make the impermanent bear weight.

Anattā — no fixed self. This is the sharpest break with the surrounding Indian traditions: where the Upanishads locate an eternal ātman, Buddhism finds a bundle of processes with no unchanging owner. The self is real as a pattern and empty as a thing.

Rebirth without a soul is the resulting puzzle. The classical image is a flame passing from one candle to the next: continuity of causation with no substance transferred.

Three vehicles

Theravāda, Mahāyāna, Vajrayāna — different goals, not just different styles.

Theravāda — "the way of the elders." Dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos. Preserves the Pali Canon; the ideal is the arahant, one who attains liberation.

Mahāyāna — dominant in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. The ideal shifts to the bodhisattva, who postpones final liberation to help all beings. Adds the doctrine of śūnyatā (emptiness), given its rigorous form by Nāgārjuna in the 2nd century CE. Zen and Pure Land are Mahāyāna schools with very different methods — one stripping away technique, the other relying on devotion to Amitābha.

Vajrayāna — Tibetan and Himalayan. Accepts the Mahāyāna goal and adds tantric method: visualisation, mantra, and a teacher–student transmission treated as essential rather than optional.

On whether Buddhism is atheistic. It has no creator God, but Theravāda and Mahāyāna cosmologies are populated with devas — powerful, long-lived, and themselves subject to impermanence. "Non-theistic" is more accurate than "atheistic."

Belief, practice, prayer, and a life

Three refuges, five precepts, and a practice with no one to petition.

What is believed. The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, set out above, are the doctrinal core. The formal act of becoming a Buddhist is not assent to a creed but taking refuge in the Three Jewels — Buddham saraṇam gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge; and likewise to the Dhamma, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, the community. Recited three times, in Pali, it is the nearest equivalent to a profession of faith.

The Eightfold Path is grouped into three trainings rather than followed in sequence. Wisdom: right view, right intention. Ethical conduct: right speech, right action, right livelihood. Mental discipline: right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. All eight are cultivated together, which is why "steps" is a misleading translation.

How it is practised. Lay Buddhists undertake the Five Precepts — training rules, not commandments, and phrased as undertakings rather than prohibitions: to refrain from killing, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicants that cloud the mind. On observance days, and for those in retreat, three further precepts are added.

Monastics take far more: the Theravāda bhikkhu follows 227 rules of the Vinaya, including possessing almost nothing, eating nothing after midday, and depending entirely on alms. The relationship between monastics and laypeople is reciprocal and daily — the saṅgha receives food on the morning alms round and gives teaching in return, and lay merit-making (dāna) is a central practice, not a peripheral one.

How it prays. This is where Buddhism diverges most sharply from the theistic traditions, and where Western descriptions usually go wrong. There is no creator to petition, so what looks like prayer is doing something else.

Bowing and offering before a Buddha image are acts of respect and of training in humility, not worship of a being who can grant requests — the Buddha is dead and, in Theravāda understanding, entirely gone. Chanting of the suttas in Pali serves memorisation, calm and merit. Meditation is the real work: samatha, calming and concentrating the mind, often on the breath; and vipassanā, insight — observing arising and passing away until impermanence stops being a doctrine and becomes something noticed. Mettā bhāvanā, the cultivation of loving-kindness, is directed outward in widening circles, from oneself to a loved one to a stranger to a difficult person to all beings.

Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna practice adds a great deal — mantra recitation, visualisation, prostrations by the thousand, devotion to bodhisattvas and, in Pure Land, reliance on Amitābha that functions very much like faith in the theistic sense. The generalisation "Buddhists do not pray" is true of some schools and false of others.

What a life looks like. The rhythm is lunar. Uposatha days at the quarters of the moon bring lay people to the monastery to take extra precepts, hear teaching and meditate. Vassa, the three-month rains retreat, keeps monastics in one place — a season of intensified practice ending in Kaṭhina, when the laity offer new robes.

Vesak, the full moon of the fourth lunar month, marks the Buddha's birth, awakening and death together and is the principal festival across Theravāda countries. In Thailand and Myanmar, temporary ordination is common — many men spend weeks or months as a monk at some point, then return to lay life, which has no parallel in the Abrahamic traditions.

Death is treated as a teaching opportunity rather than a rupture. Chanting at the bedside, reflection on impermanence, and in Tibetan practice the reading of texts to guide consciousness through the bardo, the intermediate state. Merit is formally transferred to the deceased — an act that sits awkwardly with strict no-self doctrine, and which the tradition performs anyway.

Three Smaller Traditions With Outsized Influence

Numerically modest, historically decisive — and each holds a position the larger traditions do not.

Sikhism — c. 25–30 million

Founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539) in Punjab. One formless God (Ik Onkār); rejection of caste, ritualism, idol worship and priesthood; insistence that liberation is available to a householder without renunciation. Ten human Gurus, after which authority passed permanently to the scripture itself — the Guru Granth Sahib, installed as eternal Guru in 1708, and containing verses by Hindu and Muslim saints alongside the Gurus' own. Three obligations sum it up: honest work, remembrance of God, and sharing with others — expressed daily in langar, the free community kitchen open to anyone.

Jainism — c. 4–5 million

Mahāvīra (c. 599–527 BCE) is the twenty-fourth tīrthaṅkara, not a founder — the tradition understands itself as beginningless. Its central commitment, ahiṃsā, is taken further than anywhere else: strict vegetarianism, avoidance of root vegetables, some monastics sweeping the path before them. Equally distinctive is anekāntavāda, the doctrine of many-sidedness — the claim that reality exceeds any single viewpoint, illustrated by the blind men and the elephant. It is one of the earliest systematic arguments for epistemic humility in world thought, and Gandhi credited Jain teaching directly for the philosophy of non-violent resistance.

Zoroastrianism — c. 100,000–200,000

Zarathustra taught in ancient Iran; the dating is genuinely disputed, with serious estimates ranging from 1500 BCE to the 6th century BCE. Ahura Mazda is the wise creator; existence is a moral contest between truth (aša) and the lie (druj), and human choice matters to its outcome. Individual judgement, a final renovation of the world, and a bodily resurrection all appear here early. Whether these ideas influenced Second Temple Judaism and through it Christianity and Islam is one of the longest-running arguments in the history of religion — the contact is documented, the direction of borrowing is not. Now among the smallest and most endangered of the ancient traditions.

China and Japan: Where the Category Itself Bends

Confucius 551–479 BCE · Daodejing c. 4th c. BCE · Shinto, prehistoric

A Chinese family may honour Confucian obligations, consult a Daoist temple and hold a Buddhist funeral without any sense of contradiction. Western categories of exclusive membership simply do not map.

Confucianism — the human order

Kongzi (551–479 BCE) taught in a collapsing feudal order and asked how society could be repaired. The answer was cultivation of character within relationships rather than enforcement from above.

Ren — humaneness, the cardinal virtue. Li — ritual propriety, the forms through which respect becomes visible. Xiao — filial devotion, treated as the root from which all other virtue grows. The junzi — the exemplary person — replaced birth-nobility with cultivated nobility.

Whether it is a religion or an ethical philosophy has been argued for centuries. It has temples, rites and a canon; it makes almost no metaphysical claims.

Daoism — the natural order

The Dào is the way things go when nothing forces them. The Daodejing opens by conceding its own limits: the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao.

Wu wei — effortless action, or acting with the grain rather than against it. Water is the standing image: yielding, and it carves canyons.

Alongside the philosophical texts runs a full religious Daoism with deities, alchemy, monastic orders and longevity practices — a distinction Western readers often miss entirely.

Shinto, in Japan, centres on kami — presences in mountains, rivers, ancestors and exceptional things. Purification matters more than belief, and shrine visits coexist comfortably with Buddhist practice.

Indigenous and Traditional Religions

Thousands of distinct traditions, grouped under one heading only because colonial scholarship needed somewhere to put them.

Recurring features

Across Africa, the Americas, Australia, the Pacific and northern Eurasia, some patterns recur without being universal: oral transmission rather than fixed scripture; the ancestors as present participants rather than departed; land treated as sacred and specific rather than generic; ritual specialists who mediate rather than clergy who administer; and no separation of "religion" from law, medicine, kinship or agriculture.

Yoruba tradition alone — with its òrìṣà and its Ifá divination corpus of 256 odù, each with an associated body of verse — is a system of comparable complexity to any written tradition, transmitted through trained memory.

Handling the category honestly

The grouping is external. Yoruba, Lakota, Anishinaabe and Aboriginal Australian traditions have no more in common with each other than any of them has with Islam. The category exists for our convenience.

The vocabulary is loaded. "Animism," "primitive religion" and "ancestor worship" all carry nineteenth-century evolutionary assumptions about religions maturing from simple to complex. That framework has been abandoned by scholars and survives in popular writing.

They are living, not residual. Vodou, Candomblé and Santería are contemporary traditions formed under slavery, not survivals. And a great many people practise these traditions alongside Christianity or Islam rather than instead of them — which the census categories cannot represent.

How the World Prays, and What a Religious Life Costs

Belief is what a tradition says. Practice is what it asks of your morning, your money, your appetite and your calendar — and it is the more revealing of the two.

Why compare practice rather than doctrine

Doctrines are often incommensurable — asking a Buddhist what they believe about God imports a question their framework does not raise. But every tradition has to answer the same practical questions: when do you stop what you are doing? what do you say? which way do you face? what may you not eat? who marks your birth and your burial?

Those answers can be laid side by side without distortion. They also show something doctrine hides: how different two traditions with similar beliefs can feel to live inside, and how similar two with incompatible beliefs can look from the street.

The pattern worth noticing. The traditions with a personal creator God — Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Sikhism — all pray in ways that address someone. The traditions without one — Buddhism, Jainism — perform outwardly similar acts that are internally understood as training or salutation rather than address. And Hinduism does both, depending on the school. An observer photographing all of them would produce very similar images and would have understood almost nothing.

Every tradition marks the same four moments. What each chooses to say at them is one of the most direct statements it makes about what a person is.

What these tables flatten. Every row describes a normative mainstream that a great many adherents do not follow closely, and every tradition contains communities that would fill its cells differently — a Reform Jew, a Quaker, an Ismaili Muslim and a Zen practitioner would each recognise their tradition's name and dispute the description. Lived religion is also layered with local custom that the textbooks class as folk practice and that participants simply class as religion. Treat these as a map of what each tradition asks at its most articulate, not as a survey of what people do.

Mysticism: The Family Resemblance, and Its Limits

The contemplative streams of very different traditions sound remarkably alike. Whether that means they are describing the same thing is one of the most contested questions in the field.

"I have put duality away, I have seen that the two worlds are one; One I seek, One I know, One I see, One I call."

Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī (1207–1273), Dīwān-e Shams · Sufi Islam

"The eye through which I see God is the same eye through which God sees me."

Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328) · Christian apophatic tradition

"That which is the subtle essence — this whole world has that as its self. That is the truth. That is the self. Tat tvam asi — that thou art."

Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7 · Vedānta

What the parallels do and do not show. Every major tradition developed a contemplative wing — Sufism in Islam, Kabbalah in Judaism, hesychasm and the apophatic tradition in Christianity, Vedānta in Hinduism, Zen and Dzogchen in Buddhism. All describe a state in which the sense of a separate self dissolves, and all report that language fails at exactly the same point.
Where the perennialist reading overreaches. It is tempting to conclude that mystics of all traditions reach the same summit by different paths — a view associated with Aldous Huxley and Frithjof Schuon. Scholars including Steven Katz have argued forcefully against it: experience is shaped by the concepts brought to it, and a Buddhist practitioner realising anattā (no self) and a Vedāntin realising ātman is Brahman (eternal self) are not describing one experience in two dialects. They are reporting incompatible things. The resemblance is real and worth noticing; the conclusion that all religions secretly agree does not follow from it, and tends to be reached by people outside all of them.

What a table like this cannot show. Every cell above compresses centuries of internal argument into six words, and each tradition contains schools that would object to its own row. More importantly, the columns are not really parallel — Judaism organises around a people and a practice, Christianity around a person and an event, Buddhism around a method. Asking each "what happens after death?" imports a Christian question and then reports that some traditions answer it thinly. The table is a map, drawn at a scale where the cities are dots.

What to Make of the Fact That They Disagree

The traditions make incompatible claims about the same subject matter. Every serious response to that fact has a cost.

1. Exclusivism

One tradition is true; where others conflict with it, they are mistaken. Strength: takes the actual content of the claims seriously — the traditions themselves say incompatible things, and this position does not pretend otherwise. Difficulty: the vast majority of humanity, including people of evident integrity and intelligence, is then simply wrong about the most important question there is — largely as an accident of birthplace.

2. Inclusivism

One tradition is fully true, and others contain genuine partial truth oriented towards it. Karl Rahner's "anonymous Christians" and several Qur'anic readings of the ahl al-kitāb take this shape. Strength: honours what is evidently good in other traditions without abandoning one's own. Difficulty: it reinterprets others in terms they would reject — a Buddhist does not consider herself an incomplete anything.

3. Pluralism

John Hick's position: the traditions are culturally conditioned responses to one ultimate reality, none of them privileged. Strength: explains why sanctity and moral transformation appear at similar rates across all of them. Difficulty: it requires every tradition to be wrong about its own central claim — and to accept a philosophical framework none of them taught. It is arguably a new position that relativises all the others rather than a neutral referee between them.

4. Naturalism

The traditions are human products — explicable by cognitive science, social function and history — and none is describing anything real beyond that. Strength: a single parsimonious explanation for the diversity, the conflict and the geographic correlation. Difficulty: explaining how a belief arose does not establish that it is false, and this position has to account for religious experience and moral insight without dismissing them by fiat.

Where this page stands. It does not adjudicate. Presenting each tradition in its own vocabulary is a scholarly discipline, not a claim that they are all equally true — and the deliberate refusal to rank them here should not be read as a covert vote for pluralism, which is itself one contested option among four. The traditions genuinely contradict one another on questions where at most one can be right. That is a feature of the landscape, not a defect in the description of it, and anyone who tells you it dissolves under closer study has not looked closely.
The comparative study of religion does not require you to hold no position. It requires you to be able to state someone else's position in terms they would recognise before you disagree with it. That is a harder discipline than either partisanship or indifference, and it is the only one that produces understanding.

Theology

God, Revelation, Evil, and the Long Argument Between Faith and Reason

Pillar Three: Systematic and Philosophical Theology

Theology: Faith Seeking Understanding

"I do not seek to understand in order that I may believe, but I believe in order that I may understand." — Anselm of Canterbury, Proslogion, 1078

Theology is what happens when a tradition stops reciting its claims and starts interrogating them. It is an argumentative discipline with its own standards of rigour, and the strongest objections to any doctrine were usually written by theologians rather than by outsiders. This page follows the arguments — for God, against God, and about what would follow either way — and reports where each one actually stands.

How to read this page

Every argument here is given in two panels: the case as its best defenders make it, then the strongest objection it faces. Neither panel is a straw man, and no section concludes with a verdict — because none of these arguments has produced one that the field accepts.

The material draws on Islamic, Christian, Jewish and philosophical sources roughly in proportion to where the sharpest work was done. If you want the traditions described rather than argued about, start with Religion instead.

Jump to a question What Theology Is Does the Universe Need a Cause? Fine-Tuning The Ontological Argument The Problem of Evil Divine Attributes Revelation Science & Faith Divine Hiddenness Timeline

Three Disciplines People Confuse

Theology, religious studies and philosophy of religion ask overlapping questions from three genuinely different positions. Knowing which one you are reading changes what counts as a good answer.

Inside Theology · reasons from within a tradition's commitments
Outside Religious studies · describes without adjudicating
Neither Philosophy of religion · argues from shared premises only
Why the distinction matters. "God is one" is a premise in theology, a reported belief in religious studies, and a conclusion requiring defence in philosophy of religion. A criticism that lands against one may be irrelevant to another. Most of this page sits in the third mode — arguments that do not presuppose the conclusion — with the theological material clearly marked where it appears.

Does the Universe Need a Cause?

al-Kindī, 9th c. · al-Ghazālī, 11th c. · Aquinas, 13th c. · Craig, 1979

The oldest argument in natural theology, and the one that has changed least: something began, and beginnings require explanation.

The case, at its strongest

The kalām form, developed in Islamic theology and given its modern statement by William Lane Craig, is three lines:

  • Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
  • The universe began to exist.
  • Therefore the universe has a cause.

Al-Ghazālī defended the second premise on philosophical grounds — that an actually infinite past cannot be traversed — centuries before cosmology found a beginning to date. Big Bang cosmology and the Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem (2003), which shows that any universe expanding on average must have a past boundary, are read as independent support.

Aquinas' version is different and often misreported. His concern was not a first cause in time but a sustaining cause now — why anything continues to exist at all, at this instant. He explicitly held that a universe eternal into the past would still require this.

The objections that bite
  • The first premise is an induction from within the universe. Every causal relation we have observed occurs inside space and time. Extending it to the origin of space and time may be an illegitimate extrapolation.
  • Quantum events complicate causation. Radioactive decay has no determining cause of its timing. Whether that is genuine acausality or hidden structure depends on which interpretation of quantum mechanics you hold — which is itself unsettled.
  • "Cause" is doing heavy lifting. Even granting the conclusion, the argument delivers something timeless, spaceless and immensely powerful. Getting from there to a personal God who cares what you do requires additional arguments the syllogism does not supply.
  • The BGV theorem is about classical spacetime. Its authors differ among themselves about its metaphysical implications, and it does not by itself establish creation from nothing.
A recurring failure mode on both sides. Theists sometimes present Big Bang cosmology as scientific confirmation of Genesis; atheists sometimes present quantum fluctuation models as showing the universe came from "nothing." Both misuse the physics. The vacuum of quantum field theory is a structured physical state with laws and energy — a very long way from the philosophical nothing at issue. The argument has to be settled on philosophical grounds, and it has not been.

Fine-Tuning: The Argument That Got Stronger

Paley 1802 · destroyed by Darwin 1859 · rebuilt from physics, 1970s onwards

The old design argument pointed at the eye, and evolution answered it. The new one points at the constants that make chemistry possible at all — and evolution cannot answer that, because it presupposes it.

What is actually claimed

Several physical parameters appear to sit in narrow ranges compatible with complex structure:

  • The cosmological constant. Quantum field theory's naive estimate exceeds the observed value by some 120 orders of magnitude — often called the worst prediction in physics. Larger, and no galaxy forms.
  • The strong nuclear force. Shift it a few per cent and either hydrogen fuses away entirely or heavy elements never form.
  • The carbon resonance. Fred Hoyle predicted a specific excited state of carbon-12 in 1953 purely because carbon exists in quantity. It was found. Hoyle, an atheist, called it a "put-up job."
  • Initial entropy. Roger Penrose's estimate of the improbability of the universe's initial low-entropy state is a number with an exponent that itself has an exponent.
Four serious replies
  • The multiverse. If vast numbers of universes exist with varying constants, observers necessarily find themselves in a hospitable one. Eternal inflation and string theory's landscape supply independent motivation — but no direct evidence, and critics reasonably ask whether it is testable.
  • We don't know the sample space. Calling a value improbable requires a probability distribution over possible values. We have no idea whether the constants could have been otherwise, or whether a deeper theory fixes them.
  • Observer selection. Only a universe permitting observers can be observed. Whether this dissolves the puzzle or merely restates it is genuinely disputed among philosophers of science.
  • Fine-tuned for what? The universe is overwhelmingly hostile to life — near-vacuum, near-absolute-zero, lethal radiation. "Tuned for life" describes an extraordinarily thin exception.
Why this one is worth taking seriously. Unlike Paley's watch, the fine-tuning observation is not disputed — physicists across the philosophical spectrum agree the parameters are strikingly constrained. What is disputed is entirely the inference drawn from it. That makes it the rare theological argument where the empirical premise is largely settled and the whole disagreement is about interpretation.

The Ontological Argument: The One That Refuses to Die

Anselm 1078 · Gaunilo's reply, immediately · Kant 1781 · Gödel's version, 1970

An argument for God's existence from the concept of God alone, requiring no observation of the world. Almost everyone thinks it fails. Nobody agrees on where.

The argument, and three centuries of objection

Anselm, Gaunilo's island, Kant's move, and Gödel's formalisation.

Anselm. God is "that than which nothing greater can be conceived." Suppose such a being exists only in the understanding. Then we could conceive a greater one — the same being existing in reality. But that contradicts the definition. So it must exist in reality.

Gaunilo, in Anselm's own lifetime. Run the same reasoning for the greatest conceivable island and you get an island. Something is wrong with the form.

Anselm's reply — islands have no intrinsic maximum. There is no greatest possible number of palm trees. Only a being with maximal properties by definition can take the argument's shape. This response is better than it is usually given credit for.

Kant's objection, still the most influential: existence is not a predicate. Saying a thing exists adds nothing to its description; it says that something answering the description obtains. If existence is not a perfection, the argument cannot get started.

The modal revival. Alvin Plantinga's version: if it is possible that a maximally great being exists, then in some possible world it does; and a maximally great being exists necessarily, so it exists in all worlds, including ours. Valid — but the premise "it is possible" is very nearly the conclusion in disguise, and someone who denies God's existence will deny it.

Gödel left a formalisation in modal logic which has been machine-verified as valid. Its axioms remain exactly as contestable as everything above. The argument's real interest is what it reveals about necessity, possibility and predication — which is why philosophers who reject it entirely still teach it.

The Problem of Evil

Epicurus, 3rd c. BCE · Hume 1779 · Rowe 1979 · unresolved

The strongest argument against classical theism, and the one every tradition has had to answer. It comes in two forms, and only one of them has been defused.

The logical problem — settled

The claim that "God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists" is a formal contradiction.

This version is now generally regarded as answered. Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence (1974) showed that the three propositions are consistent if it is even possible that God could not create free creatures who always choose rightly. The defence does not claim to be true — only possible, which is all that is needed to break a claim of strict contradiction. Most philosophers of religion on both sides accept that it works.

The evidential problem — open

The harder version does not claim contradiction. It claims that the quantity and distribution of suffering is powerful evidence against a good and omnipotent God.

William Rowe's example is a fawn burned in a forest fire, dying slowly, unwitnessed. No free will is exercised, no soul is built, no observer learns anything. Multiply by the vertebrate suffering of several hundred million years before humans existed at all.

This form remains live. It is a probabilistic argument, and it is answered — where it is answered — probabilistically.

Free-will theodicy

Moral evil is the price of genuine freedom, and freedom is a great enough good to be worth it. Strength: accounts for human cruelty and preserves moral responsibility. Difficulty: says nothing about earthquakes, childhood cancer, or animal suffering — and if heaven contains free beings who never sin, the assumed trade-off looks avoidable.

Soul-making (Irenaeus, Hick)

A world without hardship could not produce courage, compassion or growth. The universe is a "vale of soul-making," not a pleasure garden. Strength: matches how moral character actually develops. Difficulty: much suffering destroys people rather than forming them, and the distribution is grotesquely unequal.

Sceptical theism

We are not positioned to judge whether apparently pointless suffering has a justifying reason. A toddler cannot see why the surgery is necessary. Strength: directly targets the inference from "we see no reason" to "there is none." Difficulty: the same scepticism undermines confidence in any claim about God's goodness — and threatens ordinary moral reasoning, since it implies we may be wrong about which acts are terrible.

The traditions' own answers

Islam frames life as ibtilāʾ, trial: "We will surely test you" (2:155), with justice completed in the hereafter rather than here. Judaism gives Job, where God's answer is not an explanation but a question — and the friends who offer theodicies are the ones rebuked. Christianity points to a God who enters the suffering rather than explaining it. Buddhism dissolves the question by declining the premise of a creator, locating suffering in craving. Each answer is coherent within its own frame and unpersuasive outside it.

An honest note on this section. The problem of evil is not a puzzle for seminar rooms. For most people who encounter it, it arrives through a bereavement rather than a book, and no argument above is offered as adequate to that. Philosophy can assess whether a set of propositions is consistent. It cannot make a loss bearable, and theologians who have written best on this — from the author of Job onward — have generally said so.

Divine Attributes and Their Paradoxes

Each classical attribute of God generates a puzzle. The interesting part is that the sharpest formulations came from believers refining the doctrine, not from critics attacking it.

AttributeThe puzzleHow theologians have answered
Omnipotence Can God make a stone too heavy to lift? Either answer seems to name something God cannot do. Aquinas: omnipotence covers everything logically possible; a self-contradictory task names no task at all. The question is grammar posing as theology. Some Islamic theologians instead affirm that God's power is unbounded by human logic — a genuinely different route.
Omniscience If God infallibly knows what you will do tomorrow, can you do otherwise? Four live options. Boethius: God is outside time and sees all moments at once, so foreknowledge is not fore-. Molinism: God knows what any free creature would freely do in any circumstance. Open theism: the future's free acts are not yet objects of knowledge. Compatibilism: foreknowledge and freedom were never in conflict. Each has a cost, and this remains one of the most active disputes in the field.
Omnibenevolence Is an act good because God commands it, or commanded because it is good? (Plato's Euthyphro.) The first horn makes morality arbitrary; the second makes it independent of God. The standard reply grasps neither: goodness is identical with God's nature, so the dilemma poses a false choice. Whether that is a solution or a restatement is argued to this day.
Simplicity Classical theism holds God has no parts — power, knowledge and goodness are not components but one identical reality. Central to Aquinas, Maimonides and Ibn Sīnā alike. It protects divine unity, and it makes ordinary language about God analogical rather than literal. Critics argue it renders God abstract and hard to reconcile with a personal being who responds.
Immutability If God cannot change, how can God respond to prayer, or become incarnate, or be moved by suffering? Classical theism: God's relation to us changes without God changing — as a pillar becomes "to your left" when you move. Process theology rejects this outright and holds that God is genuinely affected by the world, at the cost of departing from the classical tradition entirely.
Transcendence If God is utterly unlike creation, how can any human word apply? The apophatic tradition — Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides, Ibn ʿArabī — says we know what God is not. Aquinas' doctrine of analogy is the middle path: "good" applied to God is neither identical to nor unrelated to its ordinary sense. The Qur'anic formula laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ — "there is nothing like unto Him" (42:11) — sets the same constraint.

Revelation: How a Tradition Claims to Know

Every scriptural religion claims access to information not available by ordinary means. They disagree sharply about what that access is like — and the difference determines how each text must be read.

Three models of inspiration

Verbal. The words themselves are divine. The Islamic position on the Qur'an: God's speech in Arabic, the Prophet the recipient rather than the author. This is why translation is called interpretation and recitation is itself an act of worship.

Dynamic. God moves human authors who write in their own idiom, vocabulary and historical situation. The mainstream Christian account of the biblical texts, which is why Paul's Greek differs from Luke's and both are held to be inspired.

Encounter. Revelation is an event, and scripture is the community's faithful witness to it. Much of modern liberal theology, and the position with the least difficulty accommodating textual criticism.

The problems each has to solve

Transmission. Manuscripts vary. Islamic scholarship developed isnād criticism for hadith and the science of qirāʾāt for canonical recitations; biblical scholarship developed textual criticism across roughly 5,800 Greek manuscripts. Both are technical disciplines, largely developed from inside the traditions.

Interpretation. A revealed text still has to be read. Tafsīr, midrash, patristic exegesis and modern hermeneutics all exist because the meaning of a text is not self-evident, and every tradition has fought over literal versus figurative reading.

Verification. Claims of self-authentication — the Qur'anic challenge of iʿjāz, or the "internal witness of the Spirit" — are compelling from inside and carry little weight outside. Miracle-based verification runs into Hume's objection that testimony to a miracle is always less probable than error in the testimony.

Science and Faith: Four Models, Honestly Assessed

Ian Barbour's taxonomy, 1990 — still the standard framing

The relationship is usually described as a war. The historical record does not support that, and neither does the current demographic data — but the alternatives have their own problems.

1. Conflict

The two make competing claims about the same reality; one must give way. Held by: both new atheists and young-earth creationists, who agree about the structure and differ only on which side wins. Difficulty: the historical evidence is against it. The "warfare" narrative was largely constructed by Draper (1874) and White (1896) and has been dismantled by historians of science since. Galileo's case involved patronage, papal politics and personal insult at least as much as doctrine, and the Church funded astronomy throughout.

2. Independence

Stephen Jay Gould's "non-overlapping magisteria": science covers fact and mechanism, religion covers meaning and value. Strength: ends the territorial dispute cleanly. Difficulty: few believers accept it, because most traditions make claims that are factual — a resurrection, a revelation at a place and date. Confining religion to values is a concession the religions themselves have not made.

3. Dialogue

The domains are distinct but adjacent, and each raises questions the other is asked about — Big Bang cosmology and creation, neuroscience and the soul, evolution and human dignity. Strength: describes what actually happens in serious work on both sides. Difficulty: it is a description of a conversation rather than a resolution of anything.

4. Integration

Theology should be reformulated in light of science — natural theology, process theology, and theistic evolution take this route. Strength: intellectually ambitious, and it treats scientific findings as genuinely informative for doctrine. Difficulty: it ties theology to the current state of science, which changes. A doctrine harmonised with the physics of 1920 needed rewriting by 1930.

Two data points that complicate the popular picture. Historically, Ibn al-Haytham, al-Bīrūnī, Copernicus, Kepler, Newton, Mendel, Faraday and Lemaître — the priest who proposed what became the Big Bang — were all religious, and several described their work in explicitly theological terms. Demographically, surveys of scientists consistently find lower religious affiliation than the general population but far from unanimity, with substantial variation by discipline and country. Neither fact settles anything about whether the claims are true. Both should make anyone cautious about the war story.
Where the specific arguments live. The detailed correlation of cosmology, geology and biology with Qur'anic, Hadith and Biblical material — including a frank treatment of where those correlations have been overstated — is worked through epoch by epoch in Before Adam.

Divine Hiddenness

J. L. Schellenberg, 1993 — the newest major argument in the field

Not why there is evil, but why there is ambiguity. If a loving God wanted relationship with us, why is the evidence so evenly balanced that sincere people reach opposite conclusions?

The argument

A perfectly loving God would ensure that anyone capable of relationship, and open to it, could have it. Relationship requires belief that the other exists. Yet there are people who sincerely seek and do not find — "non-resistant non-believers." So either they do not exist, or such a God does not.

What gives the argument force is that it does not depend on suffering, and it cannot be answered by the free-will defence: knowing someone exists does not compel you to love them.

The replies
  • Epistemic distance (Hick). Overwhelming evidence would coerce; the space for a free response requires that God not be obvious.
  • The seeking is the point. Several traditions treat the search itself as formative — the Sufi journey, the dark night of the soul, the Psalms' repeated "how long?"
  • Hiddenness is a scriptural theme, not an embarrassment. "Verily, thou art a God that hidest thyself" (Isaiah 45:15) is in the text, not a concession to critics.
  • The category is disputed. Some theists argue genuinely non-resistant non-belief is rarer than claimed — a reply many find unconvincing and somewhat presumptuous about other people's inner lives.

Theology's Turning Points

WhenWhoWhat changed
c. 400AugustineEvil as privation rather than substance; original sin; the interior turn that shapes all later Western theology
9th–10th c.Muʿtazila and al-AshʿarīIslam's foundational dispute over whether reason or revelation determines what is good — and whether the Qur'an is created or eternal
1078AnselmThe ontological argument; "faith seeking understanding" as a programme
1095al-GhazālīIncoherence of the Philosophers — a devastating internal critique of Aristotelian philosophy, and a defence of God's direct causal role
1190MaimonidesGuide for the Perplexed; radical negative theology — we can say only what God is not
1265–74Thomas AquinasSumma Theologiae: the fullest synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine, and the Five Ways
1517Martin LutherScripture over church authority; justification by faith. Western theology fragments and diversifies
1779David HumeDialogues Concerning Natural Religion — still the sharpest attack on the design argument ever written
1781Immanuel KantExistence is not a predicate; the limits of pure reason in metaphysics. Natural theology never fully recovers its confidence
1859Charles DarwinRemoves the need for design in biology, and forces theology to relocate its arguments
1919Karl BarthEpistle to the Romans: rejection of natural theology altogether; revelation as the only route
1974Alvin PlantingaThe free-will defence closes the logical problem of evil; analytic philosophy of religion is revived
1993J. L. SchellenbergDivine hiddenness — the first genuinely new argument against theism in a long time
No argument on this page settles the question, and any page claiming otherwise is selling something. What theology offers instead is precision about what is being claimed, what would follow if it were true, and what it would cost to deny it. That is worth having whichever way you come down.
