Rekhta

The Urdu Literary Tradition — Its Language, Its Ghazal, and How to Read It

Pillar Seven: Urdu and Persian Letters

Rekhta: The Scattered Language

"Rekhta ke tumhīñ ustād nahīñ ho Ghālib / kahte haiñ agle zamāne meñ koī Mīr bhī thā" — Mirza Ghalib, conceding the crown to Mir Taqi Mir

Rekhta means "scattered" or "poured together" — a language mixed from Persian, Arabic, Turkish and the Hindavi of Delhi, and for two centuries the name of what we now call Urdu. It produced one of the world's great poetic traditions, built almost entirely on a single form. This page explains how that form works, so that a reader with no Urdu can follow what a couplet is doing and why an audience shouts back at it.

How to read this page

Every couplet appears three times: the Urdu script, then a transliteration you can read aloud, then a plain translation. Say the transliteration out loud even if the sounds are unfamiliar — the ghazal is a heard form, and half its effect is in the rhyme landing where you have learned to expect it.

The section on how a ghazal is built is the key to everything else. The lexicon near the end decodes the recurring images — once you know that the tavern and the preacher are fixed characters in a repertory company, whole poems open at once.

Jump to a topic Where the Language Came From How a Ghazal Is Built The Other Forms Classical Poets Pakistani Poets Complete Poems The Lexicon The Mushaira The Modern Turn Timeline Where to Start
~230m Speakers, first and second language
2 Lines in a sher — a complete poem
19 Classical metres in common use
1857 The year that ends the classical age

Where the Language Came From

13th century Delhi → the Deccan → back to Delhi, 1700

A camp language became a court language, was exiled south, matured for three hundred years, and returned to conquer the capital that had ignored it.

The formation

Persian-speaking administrators, Turkic soldiers and the Hindavi-speaking population of the Delhi region produced a contact language from around the 13th century. Its grammar and core vocabulary are Indo-Aryan — the everyday words for water, hand, house and go are all local. Its prestige register, its poetic vocabulary and its script are Persian.

It carried many names: Hindavi, Dehlavi, Dakhni, Rekhta, Hindustani, and eventually Urdu — from the Turkish ordu, meaning camp, the same root that gives English "horde."

Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), poet, musician and disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, wrote verses alternating Persian and Hindavi lines — the earliest literary use of the mixture, and still sung at shrines seven hundred years later.

The southern detour

When the Delhi Sultanate pushed into the Deccan, the language went with it and flourished at the courts of Bijapur and Golconda as Dakhni — producing a literature of its own while Delhi's elite still wrote poetry only in Persian.

The turning point is around 1700. The divan of Wali Dakhni reached Delhi and demonstrated that serious ghazal could be written in this language. Within a generation the Delhi literati abandoned Persian for it, and the classical age began.

On Urdu and Hindi. At the level of ordinary speech they are one language — a Lahore shopkeeper and a Delhi shopkeeper understand each other completely. They diverge in script (Perso-Arabic versus Devanagari) and in which learned vocabulary they reach for (Persian and Arabic versus Sanskrit). The split is real, politically consequential, and largely a product of the nineteenth century onward.

How a Ghazal Is Built

Five technical terms unlock the entire form. Learn them once and every ghazal becomes legible.

TermWhat it isWhy it matters
SherOne couplet — two lines, called misraThe basic unit, and a complete poem in itself. This is the single hardest thing for a Western reader to accept: consecutive couplets in a ghazal need have nothing to do with one another
RadifThe refrain — an identical word or phrase ending qualifying linesThe audience learns it in the opening couplet and then anticipates it. The pleasure is in how differently each couplet arrives at the same landing
QafiaThe rhyming word immediately before the radifChanges each couplet while the radif stays fixed. Together they set a constraint the poet must satisfy five to fifteen times
MatlaThe opening couplet, in which both lines carry the rhyme and refrainAnnounces the pattern. Everything after it follows the rule in the second line only
MaqtaThe closing couplet, containing the poet's takhallus or pen nameThe signature. Ghalib addresses himself by name, often mockingly, which lets the poet appear as a character inside his own poem
BeherThe metre — quantitative, counting long and short syllablesInherited from Arabic and Persian prosody. Every line of a ghazal must scan identically, which is why ghazals are singable and why a mismatched line is instantly audible to a trained audience

One ghazal, taken apart

Ghalib's most famous opening, with the machinery labelled.

ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
بہت نکلے مرے ارمان لیکن پھر بھی کم نکلے

hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle

"A thousand desires, each one worth dying for. Many of my longings were fulfilled — and still, too few."

Mirza Ghalib · the matla

The radif is nikle — a verb meaning emerged, came out, went forth. It ends both lines here, and will end the second line of every couplet that follows.

The qafia is the rhyme before it: dam, kam, and later ham, ġham, Adam. The constraint is now fixed and the audience can hear it coming.

The wordplay is untranslatable and worth explaining. Dam nikalnā literally means "the breath goes out" — to die. So the first line says both "desires so strong the breath departs at each" and, with the same words, "each desire is worth expiring for." Ghalib then reuses nikle in its ordinary sense — longings that "came out," were fulfilled. One word, two registers, in adjacent lines.

Where the ghazal ends is the maqta, and Ghalib signs it by turning on himself:

ہوئی مدت کہ غالبؔ مر گیا پر یاد آتا ہے
وہ ہر اک بات پر کہنا کہ یوں ہوتا تو کیا ہوتا

huī muddat ki 'ġhālib' mar gayā par yaad aatā hai
vo har ik baat par kahnā ki yuuñ hotā to kyā hotā

"It's been an age since Ghalib died, but one still remembers — how he'd say, at every single thing: and what if it had been otherwise?"

Mirza Ghalib · a maqta, writing his own epitaph while alive

Why the couplets are independent. A ghazal is not an argument that develops; it is a set of variations on a constraint. This makes it perfectly suited to performance — a single sher can be quoted alone, applied to a new situation, and remain complete. It is why Urdu couplets circulate through ordinary conversation, political speech and film in a way that whole poems in other traditions do not. Agha Shahid Ali, introducing the form to American poets, described each couplet as "a stone from a necklace" which must "continue to shine in that vivid isolation."

Beyond the Ghazal

The ghazal dominates, but it is one form among several — and the alternatives were invented precisely because the ghazal cannot sustain a single argument.

Nazm

A poem on one subject, developed continuously — the opposite of the ghazal's independence. It became the vehicle for anything requiring sustained thought: Iqbal's philosophical poems, and the entire political poetry of the twentieth century. If a poet wanted to say something about Kashmir, partition or labour, the nazm was the form available.

Marsiya

Elegy for the martyrs of Karbala, recited in Muharram. Mir Anis (1803–1874) and Mirza Dabeer developed it into an epic form of hundreds of six-line stanzas, with battle description, character portraiture and lament sustained at extraordinary length. Anis is regarded by many critics as the finest narrative poet in the language, and is almost unknown outside the tradition.

Qasida, Masnavi, Rubai

Qasida — the long formal ode, usually of praise, inherited from Arabic. Masnavi — rhymed couplets used for narrative; Mir Hasan's Sihr-ul-Bayan is the classic Urdu romance. Rubai — a self-contained quatrain rhyming aaba, the form Khayyam made famous in Persian, used for compressed philosophical statement.

Dastan and the prose tradition

Dastan-goi, the art of oral storytelling, produced the Dastan-e Amir Hamza — which in its full Urdu recension runs to some forty-six volumes, one of the longest single narrative cycles in world literature. Ghalib's letters, meanwhile, did for Urdu prose what nothing else had: they abandoned ornate Persianate convention for the register of a man talking to a friend, and every later Urdu prose writer is in their debt.

The Classical Poets

Delhi and Lucknow · 1720s to 1900

Nine figures carry the classical tradition. Each is quoted here the way readers actually meet them — one couplet at a time, with the script, a transliteration to read aloud, and a plain translation.

Mir Taqi Mir (1723–1810) — Khuda-e-sukhan, the god of poetry

Plain language, unbearable feeling. Ghalib's own measure of greatness.

Born in Agra, orphaned young, driven from Delhi by the sack of 1739 and the disorder that followed, and dependent all his life on patrons he despised. Mir wrote in a deliberately simple register at a time when ornament was expected, and the plainness is what makes the grief land.

ہستی اپنی حباب کی سی ہے
یہ نمائش سراب کی سی ہے

hastī apnī habāb kī sī hai
ye numā.ish sarāb kī sī hai

"Our existence is like a bubble on water. This whole display is the appearance of a mirage."

Mir Taqi Mir

پتا پتا بوٹا بوٹا حال ہمارا جانے ہے
جانے نہ جانے گل ہی نہ جانے باغ تو سارا جانے ہے

patta patta būṭā būṭā hāl hamārā jāne hai
jāne na jāne gul hī na jāne bāġh to sārā jāne hai

"Every leaf, every shrub knows the state I am in. The rose alone may not know it — but the whole garden does."

Mir Taqi Mir · his most quoted line

The trick here is entirely structural. A long, loose metre lets the repetition — patta patta, būṭā būṭā — spread outward like the rumour it describes, and the second line then contracts to a single exception. The beloved is the last to know, and everyone else has known for some time.

دکھائی دیے یوں کہ بے خود کیا
ہمیں آپ سے بھی جدا کر چلے

dikhā.ī diye yuuñ ki be-ḳhud kiyā
hameñ āp se bhī judā kar chale

"You appeared in such a way that I was taken out of myself — you left, having separated me even from me."

Mir Taqi Mir

راہ دور عشق میں روتا ہے کیا
آگے آگے دیکھیے ہوتا ہے کیا

rāh-e-dūr-e-ishq meñ rotā hai kyā
āge āge dekhiye hotā hai kyā

"Why weep so early on the long road of love? Wait and see what happens further along."

Mir Taqi Mir

Mir's other great subject is the city itself. He lived through the destruction of Mughal Delhi, and his poetry is among the earliest sustained literature of displacement in South Asia — a set of themes that would be needed again in 1857, and again in 1947.

Mirza Sauda (1713–1781) — the satirist and the grand ode

The third of the great trio, and the one who could wound.

Mir's contemporary and rival, and the master of the qasida — the long formal ode — at a time when Mir was perfecting the ghazal. Sauda is also the tradition's great satirist, and his hajv could end a reputation.

گل پھینکے ہے اوروں کی طرف بلکہ ثمر بھی
اے خانہ برانداز چمن کچھ تو ادھر بھی

gul pheñke hai auroñ kī taraf balki samar bhī
ai ḳhāna-bar-andāz-e-chaman kuchh to idhar bhī

"You throw flowers to others — fruit, even. O you who wrecked the garden's household: something this way too."

Mirza Muhammad Rafi Sauda

The complaint is addressed to the beloved, to fortune and to God at once, and the tone is closer to a grievance filed than a lament. That worldly, argumentative register is what separates Sauda from Mir, and it is why the two were read as opposites in their own lifetime.

Khwaja Mir Dard (1721–1785) — the mystic of the trio

A Sufi shaikh who wrote the ghazal as devotional practice.

Where Mir gives grief and Sauda gives argument, Dard gives the tradition its purest mystical voice. He was a practising Naqshbandi shaikh, and in his verse the ambiguity between the human and divine beloved barely operates — the beloved is God, and the poem is close to a form of remembrance.

جگ میں آ کر ادھر ادھر دیکھا
تو ہی آیا نظر جدھر دیکھا

jag meñ ā kar idhar udhar dekhā
tū hī āyā nazar jidhar dekhā

"Having come into the world, I looked here and there — wherever I looked, it was only You I saw."

Khwaja Mir Dard

تہمتیں چند اپنے ذمے دھر چلے
جس لیے آئے تھے سو ہم کر چلے

tuhmateñ chand apne zimme dhar chale
jis liye aa.e the so ham kar chale

"We took a few accusations upon ourselves and moved on. What we came for — that, we did."

Khwaja Mir Dard

Mirza Ghalib (1797–1869) — difficulty as a virtue

He thought his Persian was better. Posterity disagreed.

Born in Agra, resident in Delhi, perpetually in debt, fond of wine and mangoes, and convinced his reputation would rest on his Persian work. It rests instead on a slim Urdu divan he half dismissed.

Ghalib's characteristic move is metaphysical compression: a couplet that appears to be about a lover turns out to be about existence, causation or God, and refuses to settle on one.

نہ تھا کچھ تو خدا تھا کچھ نہ ہوتا تو خدا ہوتا
ڈبویا مجھ کو ہونے نے نہ ہوتا میں تو کیا ہوتا

na thā kuchh to ḳhudā thā kuchh na hotā to ḳhudā hotā
duboyā mujh ko hone ne na hotā maiñ to kyā hotā

"When there was nothing, there was God; had there been nothing, God would still be. Being is what drowned me — had I not been, what would I have been?"

Mirza Ghalib · possibly the most argued-over couplet in the language

Two lines that stage the whole problem of contingent existence — why anything at all rather than nothing — and then turn it into a personal complaint. Commentators have read it as Sufi ontology, as near-blasphemy, and as a joke at his own expense. The couplet supports all three and settles on none.

عشق پر زور نہیں ہے یہ وہ آتش غالبؔ
کہ لگائے نہ لگے اور بجھائے نہ بنے

ishq par zor nahīñ hai ye vo ātish 'ġhālib'
ki lagā.e na lage aur bujhā.e na bane

"There is no forcing love, Ghalib — it is that kind of fire: you cannot light it by wanting to, and you cannot put it out."

Mirza Ghalib

دل ہی تو ہے نہ سنگ و خشت درد سے بھر نہ آئے کیوں
روئیں گے ہم ہزار بار کوئی ہمیں ستائے کیوں

dil hī to hai na sañg o ḳhisht dard se bhar na aa.e kyuuñ
ro.eñge ham hazār bār koī hameñ satā.e kyuuñ

"It is only a heart, not brick and stone — why should it not fill with pain? I will weep a thousand times; why should anyone torment me for it?"

Mirza Ghalib

قید حیات و بند غم اصل میں دونوں ایک ہیں
موت سے پہلے آدمی غم سے نجات پائے کیوں

qaid-e-hayāt o band-e-ġham asl meñ donoñ ek haiñ
maut se pahle ādmī ġham se najāt pā.e kyuuñ

"The prison of life and the chains of grief are, in truth, one thing. Why should a man be released from sorrow before he is released from living?"

Mirza Ghalib · from the same ghazal as the couplet above

بازیچۂ اطفال ہے دنیا مرے آگے
ہوتا ہے شب و روز تماشا مرے آگے

bāzīcha-e-atfāl hai duniyā mire āge
hotā hai shab-o-roz tamāshā mire āge

"The world is a children's playground before me — night and day, a spectacle plays out in front of me."

Mirza Ghalib

ان کے دیکھے سے جو آ جاتی ہے منہ پر رونق
وہ سمجھتے ہیں کہ بیمار کا حال اچھا ہے

un ke dekhe se jo ā jātī hai muñh par raunaq
vo samajhte haiñ ki bīmār kā hāl achchhā hai

"Because the sight of them brings colour to my face, they conclude the patient is doing well."

Mirza Ghalib

A rare Ghalib couplet with no metaphysics in it at all — just an exact observation about being misread by the person you most want to be understood by.

1857 is the hinge of his life. He watched the uprising and its suppression from inside Delhi, saw the court he depended on abolished and friends executed, and recorded it in Dastanbuy — a diary written with one eye on the British authorities, and correspondingly hard to read straight. His letters from those years are the best prose in the language.

Momin Khan Momin (1800–1852) — the couplet Ghalib envied

Two lines Ghalib is said to have offered his whole divan for.

A physician, astrologer and chess player as well as a poet, and a contemporary of both Ghalib and Zauq. All three couplets below come from the same ghazal, on the radif nahīñ hotā — which is worth reading in sequence to see how one refrain is made to do three completely different jobs.

اثر اس کو ذرا نہیں ہوتا
رنج راحت فزا نہیں ہوتا

asar us ko zarā nahīñ hotā
ranj rāhat-fazā nahīñ hotā

"Nothing moves her in the slightest. And grief, it turns out, does not become a comfort."

Momin Khan Momin · the matla

تم مرے پاس ہوتے ہو گویا
جب کوئی دوسرا نہیں ہوتا

tum mire paas hote ho goyā
jab koī dūsrā nahīñ hotā

"You are, as it were, beside me — whenever no one else is."

Momin Khan Momin

The story that Ghalib offered his entire divan for this couplet may be apocryphal, but the admiration is not hard to understand. It holds at least three readings at once and will not release any of them: you are with me when I am alone; you are with me only in your absence, as imagination; and — the cruellest — you come to me only when no one else is available to you. Nothing in the grammar decides between them.

کیوں سنے عرض مضطر مومنؔ
صنم آخر خدا نہیں ہوتا

kyuuñ sune arz-e-muztar-e-'momin'
sanam āḳhir ḳhudā nahīñ hotā

"Why would she hear Momin's desperate petition? An idol, after all, is not God."

Momin Khan Momin · the maqta

The closing couplet does something the tradition rarely does: it breaks the ambiguity on purpose. Having spent a whole ghazal letting the beloved stand in for the divine, Momin ends by naming the difference — sanam, the idol, is not ḳhudā. It is a theological joke and a genuine complaint in the same breath.

Bahadur Shah Zafar (1775–1862) — the emperor who lost everything

The last Mughal, exiled to Rangoon. And a genuine attribution problem.

The last Mughal emperor was a serious poet with Zauq and then Ghalib as his court's leading figures. After 1857 he was tried, deposed, and exiled to Rangoon, where he died and was buried in an unmarked grave.

لگتا نہیں ہے جی مرا اجڑے دیار میں
کس کی بنی ہے عالم ناپائیدار میں

lagtā nahīñ hai jī mirā ujḌe dayār meñ
kis kī banī hai ālam-e-nā-pā.edār meñ

"My heart finds no rest in this ruined country. Whose fortunes have ever held, in a world that does not last?"

Attributed to Bahadur Shah Zafar

کتنا ہے بدنصیب ظفرؔ دفن کے لیے
دو گز زمین بھی نہ ملی کوئے یار میں

kitnā hai bad-nasīb 'zafar' dafn ke liye
do gaz zamīn bhī na milī kū-e-yār meñ

"How luckless is Zafar — for burial, he could not get even two yards of ground in the street of the beloved."

Attributed to Bahadur Shah Zafar

An honest note on attribution. This ghazal is among the most famous in the language and is very widely printed under Zafar's name, its power resting on the biographical fit — a deposed emperor with no grave in his own city. Several scholars have questioned the attribution, proposing Muztar Khairabadi or Seemab Akbarabadi instead, and it does not appear in the earliest collections of Zafar's work. The dispute is unresolved. It is quoted here because it is part of the tradition as received, with the doubt stated rather than hidden — which is also a useful reminder that a great deal of pre-modern Urdu verse circulated orally before it was ever catalogued.

Daagh Dehlvi (1831–1905) — the ease that hides the work

The most quotable of them all, and Iqbal's first teacher.

Where Ghalib is difficult, Daagh is transparent — and the transparency is engineered. He wrote in a colloquial Delhi register so idiomatic that his couplets pass for ordinary speech, which is precisely why so many of them survive in conversation. The young Iqbal sent his early verse to Daagh for correction.

خوب پردہ ہے کہ چلمن سے لگے بیٹھے ہیں
صاف چھپتے بھی نہیں سامنے آتے بھی نہیں

ḳhūb pardā hai ki chilman se lage baiṭhe haiñ
sāf chhupte bhī nahīñ sāmne aate bhī nahīñ

"Some veil this is — sitting pressed up against the blind: not quite hidden, and not quite coming out either."

Daagh Dehlvi

لطف مے تجھ سے کیا کہوں زاہد
ہائے کم بخت تو نے پی ہی نہیں

lutf-e-mai tujh se kyā kahūñ zāhid
hā.e kambaḳht tū ne pī hī nahīñ

"What can I tell you of the pleasure of wine, ascetic? Poor wretch — you have never tasted it."

Daagh Dehlvi

The second is the perfect specimen of the zāhid convention explained in the lexicon above: the pious objector exists in the ghazal only in order to be dismissed, and the wine is never only wine.

Akbar Allahabadi (1846–1921) — the satirist of colonial modernity

A judge in the colonial courts who spent his poetry mocking them.

Akbar worked inside the British Indian legal system and wrote verse attacking almost everything it stood for — English education, imported manners, and above all the new class of nationalist politician. His weapon is bathos: classical metre and diction, deployed on dinner parties and railway timetables.

قوم کے غم میں ڈنر کھاتے ہیں حکام کے ساتھ
رنج لیڈر کو بہت ہے مگر آرام کے ساتھ

qaum ke ġham meñ ḍinar khāte haiñ hukkām ke sāth
ranj līḍar ko bahut hai magar ārām ke sāth

"In grief for the nation, he dines with the officials. The leader suffers a great deal — but comfortably."

Akbar Allahabadi

Dropping the English words ḍinar and līḍar into a classical metre is the whole joke, and it is a technique no one had used before him.

دنیا میں ہوں دنیا کا طلب گار نہیں ہوں
بازار سے گزرا ہوں خریدار نہیں ہوں

duniyā meñ huuñ duniyā kā talabgār nahīñ huuñ
bāzār se guzrā huuñ ḳharīdār nahīñ huuñ

"I am in the world; I am not a seeker of it. I have walked through the marketplace — I am not a buyer."

Akbar Allahabadi

Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938) — philosophy in verse

The poet who argued with God, in metre.

Trained in philosophy at Cambridge and Munich, a barrister by profession, and the most intellectually ambitious poet the language has produced. Iqbal wrote in both Urdu and Persian and used verse as the vehicle for a worked-out philosophical position.

Shikwa (1909) and Jawab-e-Shikwa (1913) are a complaint addressed to God about the condition of Muslims, and God's reply. The first caused genuine scandal for its presumption; the pair remain among the most recited poems in the language.

خودی کو کر بلند اتنا کہ ہر تقدیر سے پہلے
خدا بندے سے خود پوچھے بتا تیری رضا کیا ہے

ḳhudī ko kar buland itnā ki har taqdīr se pahle
ḳhudā bande se ḳhud pūchhe batā terī razā kyā hai

"Raise the self so high that, before writing each destiny, God himself asks the servant: tell me, what is it you wish?"

Muhammad Iqbal · the doctrine of khudi in two lines

Khudi — usually translated "selfhood" — is his central concept: not egotism but the development of a fully realised self capable of moral action, set against both Western materialism and what he saw as a quietist misreading of Sufi self-annihilation.

ستاروں سے آگے جہاں اور بھی ہیں
ابھی عشق کے امتحاں اور بھی ہیں

sitāroñ se āge jahāñ aur bhī haiñ
abhī ishq ke imtihāñ aur bhī haiñ

"Beyond the stars there are other worlds still. There are further trials of love yet to come."

Muhammad Iqbal

تو شاہیں ہے پرواز ہے کام تیرا
ترے سامنے آسماں اور بھی ہیں

tū shāhīñ hai parvāz hai kaam terā
tire sāmne āsmāñ aur bhī haiñ

"You are a falcon; flight is your work. There are other skies in front of you."

Muhammad Iqbal · from the same ghazal

The falcon is Iqbal's signature image — solitary, disciplined, unattached to comfort, and never nesting. It stands against the caged songbird of the classical ghazal, and the substitution is the whole argument.

ہزاروں سال نرگس اپنی بے نوری پہ روتی ہے
بڑی مشکل سے ہوتا ہے چمن میں دیدہ ور پیدا

hazāroñ sāl nargis apnī be-nūrī pe rotī hai
baḌī mushkil se hotā hai chaman meñ dīda-var paidā

"For thousands of years the narcissus weeps over its own sightlessness. Only with great difficulty is one who truly sees born into the garden."

Muhammad Iqbal

جس کھیت سے دہقاں کو میسر نہیں روزی
اس کھیت کے ہر خوشۂ گندم کو جلا دو

jis khet se dahqāñ ko muyassar nahīñ rozī
us khet ke har ḳhosha-e-gandum ko jalā do

"The field that does not yield the farmer his bread — burn every ear of wheat in that field."

Muhammad Iqbal

A line the socialist poets of the next generation adopted wholesale, and one reason Iqbal is claimed by political traditions that agree on almost nothing else.

He also wrote Tarana-e-Hindi (1904) — "Sāre jahāñ se achchhā" — still sung across India, whose most quoted couplet is a plea against sectarian division:

مذہب نہیں سکھاتا آپس میں بیر رکھنا
ہندی ہیں ہم وطن ہے ہندوستاں ہمارا

mazhab nahīñ sikhātā āpas meñ bair rakhnā
hindī haiñ ham vatan hai hindostāñ hamārā

"Religion does not teach us to hold enmity among ourselves. We are of Hind; our homeland is Hindustan."

Muhammad Iqbal, 1904

He later argued for a separate Muslim political entity — a trajectory that makes him claimed and contested by more than one national tradition, and makes the 1904 poem a genuinely complicated object rather than a contradiction to be explained away.

The Pakistani Generations

1947 to the present · Lahore, Karachi, and a good deal of prison

Partition gave Urdu a state and a set of subjects it had not had before: exile, martial law, censorship, and a language arguing about who it now belonged to.

Faiz Ahmed Faiz (1911–1984) — the beloved and the cause

Imprisoned in 1951, and the most translated modern Urdu poet.

Faiz's formal achievement is precise and easy to state: he kept the entire classical vocabulary — the beloved, the tavern, the wound, the morning — and made every term carry a political sense without losing its original one. A censor reading for sedition finds a love poem.

His central statement of the method is a nazm from his first collection, Naqsh-e-Faryadi (1943), which opens by withdrawing from love itself:

مجھ سے پہلی سی محبت مرے محبوب نہ مانگ

mujh se pahlī sī mohabbat mire mahbūb na māñg

"Do not ask of me, my love, that love I once gave you."

Faiz Ahmed Faiz · Naqsh-e-Faryadi, 1943

The poem's argument is that the world's suffering has made a purely private devotion impossible — and it turns on a couplet that has become the most quoted lines he wrote:

اور بھی دکھ ہیں زمانے میں محبت کے سوا
راحتیں اور بھی ہیں وصل کی راحت کے سوا

aur bhī duḳh haiñ zamāne meñ mohabbat ke sivā
rāhateñ aur bhī haiñ vasl kī rāhat ke sivā

"There are other sorrows in the world than the sorrow of love. There are other comforts than the comfort of union."

Faiz Ahmed Faiz

بول کہ لب آزاد ہیں تیرے
بول زباں اب تک تیری ہے

bol ki lab āzād haiñ tere
bol zabāñ ab tak terī hai

"Speak, for your lips are free. Speak — your tongue is still your own."

Faiz Ahmed Faiz · Bol

Arrested in 1951 in the Rawalpindi Conspiracy Case and held for four years, much of it under sentence of death. The prison poems of Dast-e-Saba and Zindan-Nama were written in that period. His late nazm Hum Dekhenge (1979), written under Zia-ul-Haq's martial law, uses entirely Qur'anic imagery of the Day of Judgement to describe the fall of a tyrant — which made it impossible to ban on religious grounds, and it remains a protest anthem across South Asia.

Josh Malihabadi (1898–1982) — Shair-e-Inquilab

The poet of revolution, and of a vocabulary nobody else could carry.

Josh commanded a Persianised diction of extraordinary density and used it at volume — the nazm rather than the ghazal, declaimed rather than sung. He wrote against British rule with a directness that got his work banned, and migrated to Pakistan in 1958, a move he spent much of his later life ambivalent about.

کام ہے میرا تغیر نام ہے میرا شباب
میرا نعرہ انقلاب و انقلاب و انقلاب

kaam hai merā taġhayyur naam hai merā shabāb
merā na.ara inqilāb o inqilāb o inqilāb

"My work is transformation; my name is youth. My cry is revolution, and revolution, and revolution."

Josh Malihabadi

His autobiography Yaadon ki Baraat is as well known as his verse, and considerably more scandalous.

Nasir Kazmi (1925–1972) — the quiet voice after the noise

Small words, short metres, and the ghazal rebuilt from the ground up.

Kazmi migrated from Ambala in 1947 and never really wrote about anything else. His achievement was to take the ghazal back to Mir's plainness at a moment when the form was becoming either political or ornamental — short metres, everyday vocabulary, and a persistent sense of something recently lost that is never named.

دل میں اک لہر سی اٹھی ہے ابھی
کوئی تازہ ہوا چلی ہے ابھی

dil meñ ik lahr sī uṭhī hai abhī
koī tāza havā chalī hai abhī

"A kind of wave has just risen in the heart. Some fresh wind has just now begun to blow."

Nasir Kazmi

کچھ یادگار شہر ستم گر ہی لے چلیں
آئے ہیں اس گلی میں تو پتھر ہی لے چلیں

kuchh yādgār-e-shahr-e-sitamgar hī le chaleñ
aa.e haiñ is galī meñ to patthar hī le chaleñ

"Let us at least carry off some memento of the tyrant's city. Since we have come down this street, let us take the stones."

Nasir Kazmi

The stones are the ones thrown at him. Taking them as a keepsake is the entire poem, and nothing in it needs explaining.

Habib Jalib (1928–1993) — poetry for the street

Written to be shouted by a crowd, not admired in a room.

Jalib made a deliberate choice against literary difficulty. Where Faiz encoded politics inside classical metaphor, Jalib wrote in plain speech, in short singable metres, to be recited at rallies — and was imprisoned repeatedly across four decades and three military governments for it.

Dastoor (1962), written against Ayub Khan's constitution, is the best-known protest poem in the language:

دیپ جس کا محلات ہی میں جلے
چند لوگوں کی خوشیوں کو لے کر چلے

diip jis kā mahallāt hī meñ jale
chand logoñ kī ḳhushiyoñ ko le kar chale

"A lamp that burns only inside the palaces; that carries the happiness of a handful of people —"

Habib Jalib · Dastoor, 1962

ایسے دستور کو صبح بے نور کو
میں نہیں مانتا میں نہیں جانتا

aise dastūr ko subh-e-be-nūr ko
maiñ nahīñ māntā maiñ nahīñ jāntā

"Such an order, such a lightless dawn — I do not accept it, I do not acknowledge it."

Habib Jalib · the refrain of Dastoor

Note what the form is doing: this is a refrain built for a crowd to complete. The poem is engineered so that a thousand people can arrive at the last line together, which is a compositional decision, not a political one.

Ahmad Faraz (1931–2008) — the most sung of the moderns

Classical sweetness, contemporary directness, and two exiles.

Faraz is the modern poet whose ghazals most readily became songs, largely because he kept the classical music of the line while stripping out the archaic vocabulary. He read verse against Zia-ul-Haq's martial law, was arrested for it, and spent years in self-imposed exile in Britain and Canada.

رنجش ہی سہی دل ہی دکھانے کے لیے آ
آ پھر سے مجھے چھوڑ کے جانے کے لیے آ

ranjish hī sahī dil hī dukhāne ke liye ā
ā phir se mujhe chhoḌ ke jāne ke liye ā

"Let it be resentment, then — come, if only to wound me. Come, if only to leave me again."

Ahmad Faraz · sung by Mehdi Hassan

The couplet works by conceding everything in advance. There is no argument left for the beloved to win, which is why the demand is impossible to refuse and impossible to satisfy.

اب کے ہم بچھڑے تو شاید کبھی خوابوں میں ملیں
جس طرح سوکھے ہوئے پھول کتابوں میں ملیں

ab ke ham bichhḌe to shāyad kabhī ḳhvāboñ meñ mileñ
jis tarah sūkhe hue phūl kitāboñ meñ mileñ

"If we part this time, perhaps we will meet only in dreams — the way dried flowers are found inside books."

Ahmad Faraz

One image, exactly placed: pressed flowers are found by accident, long afterwards, by someone who was looking for something else. The whole couplet is that.

Parveen Shakir (1952–1994) — the ghazal in a woman's voice

Khushbu, 1976 — a debut that won the Adamjee Award and changed who the form could speak as.

Shakir did something the form had structurally resisted for three centuries. The classical ghazal's lover is grammatically masculine by convention and its beloved unreachable and abstract; Shakir wrote as a woman, in the feminine voice, about a specific person — and kept the technical rigour intact while doing it.

Khushbu (1976) was her first collection and won the Adamjee Award. Its opening ghazal makes the book's argument in two lines:

کو بہ کو پھیل گئی بات شناسائی کی
اس نے خوشبو کی طرح میری پذیرائی کی

kū-ba-kū phail ga.ī bāt shanāsā.ī kī
us ne ḳhushbū kī tarah merī pazīrā.ī kī

"Street by street, the word of our acquaintance spread. He received me the way a fragrance is received."

Parveen Shakir · Khushbu, 1976

Fragrance is the book's governing image, and it is doing precise work: it spreads without being seen, cannot be contained, and cannot be denied once present — which is also an exact description of how a woman's reputation travelled in the society she was writing in.

جگنو کو دن کے وقت پرکھنے کی ضد کریں
بچے ہمارے عہد کے چالاک ہو گئے

jugnū ko din ke vaqt parakhne kī zid kareñ
bachche hamāre ahd ke chālāk ho ga.e

"They insist on testing the firefly in daylight. The children of our age have grown cunning."

Parveen Shakir

She published Sad-barg, Khud-Kalami, Inkaar and Kaf-e-Aaina before her death in a car accident in Islamabad at forty-two.

Jaun Elia (1931–2002) — self-laceration as a method

Published his first collection at sixty, and became the most quoted poet among young readers.

A scholar of philosophy and Islamic history who wrote for four decades before allowing a collection to be printed — Shayad, in 1991, when he was sixty. His register is conversational to the point of rudeness, and the target is almost always himself.

کتنی دل کش ہو تم کتنا دل جو ہوں میں
کیا ستم ہے کہ ہم لوگ مر جائیں گے

kitnī dilkash ho tum kitnā dil-jū huuñ maiñ
kyā sitam hai ki ham log mar jā.eñge

"How captivating you are; how devoted I am. What an outrage, that people like us are going to die."

Jaun Elia · Shayad, 1991

The couplet's whole effect is in the tonal drop. Two lines of conventional ghazal flattery, then a flat statement of mortality delivered as a personal insult — and sitam, "outrage" or "tyranny," is a word the classical tradition reserves for the beloved's cruelty, here reassigned to death itself.

اب نہیں کوئی بات خطرے کی
اب سبھی کو سبھی سے خطرہ ہے

ab nahīñ koī bāt ḳhatre kī
ab sabhī ko sabhī se ḳhatrā hai

"There is nothing to worry about any more. Now everyone is a danger to everyone."

Jaun Elia

Written out of Karachi's violence in the 1980s and 1990s, and a fair example of why his popularity climbed sharply after his death.

Munir Niazi (1928–2006) and Ibn-e-Insha (1927–1978)

Two very different ways of writing simply.

Munir Niazi wrote in Urdu and Punjabi both, and built a body of work around a single recurring feeling: arriving too late, in a landscape that has already changed. His best-known nazm names it outright.

ہمیشہ دیر کر دیتا ہوں میں
ہر ضروری بات کہنی ہو
کوئی وعدہ نبھانا ہو

hamesha der kar detā huuñ maiñ
har zarūrī bāt kahnī ho
koī vāda nibhānā ho

"I am always late — whenever there is something necessary to say, or a promise to keep."

Munir Niazi · opening of Hamesha Der Kar Deta Hun Main

Ibn-e-Insha is the tradition's great humourist — a travel writer and satirist whose serious verse is disarmingly plain, and whose most famous couplet is a piece of conversational reporting.

کل چودھویں کی رات تھی شب بھر رہا چرچا ترا
کچھ نے کہا یہ چاند ہے کچھ نے کہا چہرہ ترا

kal chaudhvīñ kī rāt thī shab bhar rahā charchā terā
kuchh ne kahā ye chāñd hai kuchh ne kahā chehra terā

"Last night was the fourteenth night; all night long the talk was of you. Some said, that is the moon. Some said, that is your face."

Ibn-e-Insha

The fourteenth night of the lunar month is the full moon. The couplet takes the single most exhausted comparison in the language — beloved as moon — and rescues it by putting it in other people's mouths as a reported disagreement.

The generation still writing. Kishwar Naheed, whose Hum Gunahgar Auratein ("We Sinful Women") gave Pakistani feminist writing its title and its posture, and the late Fahmida Riaz, who wrote about the body, exile and religious authority with a frankness that got her charged with sedition and driven into exile in India for years — both extended what Shakir opened, and in a more confrontational register. Zehra Nigah, Amjad Islam Amjad, Iftikhar Arif and Kishwar Naheed have carried the mushaira tradition into a period when most of its audience now arrives by video.

The Anthology: Four Poems, Entire

Complete texts · Urdu, transliteration, translation

Single couplets are how the ghazal travels. But a ghazal is also a made object with an opening, a signature and a shape — and you cannot see that from an excerpt. Here are four complete works.

Reading a ghazal whole

Read down the right-hand edge of the transliteration first and notice the refrain arriving in the same place every time. Then read the couplets in order and notice that they are not a sequence — each is complete, and the poem is a set of variations rather than an argument. The last couplet will contain the poet's name.

Texts follow the standard scholarly editions where one exists — for Ghalib, the divan as established by Arshi and presented in Frances Pritchett's A Desertful of Roses. Where a reading is disputed, the note says so.

Mirza Ghalib — hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī

Composed 1853 · Arshi #230 · 9 verses, complete
Radif: nikle · Qafia: dam, kam, ham, ġham…
First printed in the Dihli Urdu Akhbar, 19 June 1853

The most famous ghazal in the language, and a masterclass in a single refrain. Nikalnā means to emerge, come out, be produced, be fulfilled, depart, escape, or turn out to be — and Ghalib uses a different sense in almost every couplet. Watch the word change job nine times.

1

ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
بہت نکلے مرے ارمان لیکن پھر بھی کم نکلے

hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle

A thousand desires, each one worth dying for. Many of my longings were fulfilled — and still, too few.

The matla · dam nikalnā — for the breath to leave, i.e. to die

2

ڈرے کیوں میرا قاتل کیا رہے گا اس کی گردن پر
وہ خوں جو چشم تر سے عمر بھر یوں دم بہ دم نکلے

ḍare kyuuñ merā qātil kyā rahegā us kī gardan par
vo ḳhūñ jo chashm-e-tar se umr bhar yuuñ dam ba-dam nikle

Why should my killer be afraid? What will be held against him — blood that leaked from wet eyes, breath by breath, over a whole lifetime?

A murder with no evidence, because the victim bled slowly and in private

3

نکلنا خلد سے آدم کا سنتے آئے ہیں لیکن
بہت بے آبرو ہو کر ترے کوچے سے ہم نکلے

nikalnā ḳhuld se ādam kā sunte aa.e haiñ lekin
bahut be-ābrū ho kar tire kūche se ham nikle

We have always heard about Adam's expulsion from paradise — but I left your street in far greater disgrace.

The most quoted verse of the nine

4

بھرم کھل جائے ظالم تیرے قامت کی درازی کا
اگر اس طرۂ پر پیچ و خم کا پیچ و خم نکلے

bharam khul jaa.e zālim tere qāmat kī darāzī kā
agar us turra-e-pur-pech-o-ḳham kā pech-o-ḳham nikle

The illusion of your height would be exposed, tyrant, if the coils were taken out of that coiling forelock.

Teasing, and metrically dazzling — pech-o-ḳham twice in one line

5

مگر لکھوائے کوئی اس کو خط تو ہم سے لکھوائے
ہوئی صبح اور گھر سے کان پر رکھ کر قلم نکلے

magar likhvā.e koī us ko ḳhat to ham se likhvā.e
huī subh aur ghar se kān par rakh kar qalam nikle

If anyone wants a letter written to her, they should have me write it. Morning came, and out I went, pen tucked behind my ear.

The lover as a jobbing scribe — comic, and quietly devastating

6

ہوئی اس دور میں منسوب مجھ سے بادہ آشامی
پھر آیا وہ زمانہ جو جہاں میں جام جم نکلے

huī is daur meñ mansūb mujh se bāda-āshāmī
phir āyā vo zamāna jo jahāñ meñ jām-e-jam nikle

In this age, wine-drinking has become associated with my name. That era has come round again, in which the cup of Jamshed appears in the world.

The legendary cup of the Persian king Jamshed, in which all the world could be seen

7

ہوئی جن سے توقع خستگی کی داد پانے کی
وہ ہم سے بھی زیادہ خستۂ تیغ ستم نکلے

huī jin se tavaqqoʿ ḳhastagī kī dād pāne kī
vo ham se bhī ziyāda ḳhasta-e-teġh-e-sitam nikle

Those from whom I expected some acknowledgement of my woundedness — they turned out to be more badly cut by the blade of cruelty than I was.

Here nikle means "turned out to be"

8

محبت میں نہیں ہے فرق جینے اور مرنے کا
اسی کو دیکھ کر جیتے ہیں جس کافر پہ دم نکلے

mohabbat meñ nahīñ hai farq jiine aur marne kā
usī ko dekh kar jiite haiñ jis kāfir pe dam nikle

In love there is no difference between living and dying: we stay alive by looking at the very infidel we would die for.

The couplet the whole ghazal is built to arrive at

9

کہاں میخانے کا دروازہ غالبؔ اور کہاں واعظ
پر اتنا جانتے ہیں کل وہ جاتا تھا کہ ہم نکلے

kahāñ mai-ḳhāne kā darvāza 'ġhālib' aur kahāñ vāʿiz
par itnā jānte haiñ kal vo jaatā thā ki ham nikle

What has the tavern door to do with the preacher, Ghalib? But this much we know — yesterday he was going in as we were coming out.

The maqta · the preacher caught, and the poet too polite to say so directly

The famous tenth verse that is not Ghalib's. Many printed editions, and Jagjit Singh's well-known sung version, include a verse beginning ḳhudā ke vāste pardā na kaʿbe se uṭhā vāʿiz — "for God's sake, preacher, don't lift the covering from the Kaʿbah; it may be that the same infidel idol emerges here too." It is not in Ghalib's divan. Ghalib supervised two editions after composing this ghazal and published virtually every verse he wrote, and he twice wrote furious letters repudiating verses falsely attributed to him. Frances Pritchett traces the verse instead to the Kulliyat-e-Zafar, where it appears with a slightly different first line — ḳhudā ke vāste zāhid uṭhā pardā na kaʿbe kā. It is a fine verse. It is Bahadur Shah Zafar's.

Momin Khan Momin — asar us ko zarā nahīñ hotā

15 verses, complete · Radif: nahīñ hotā · Qafia: zarā, fazā, burā, mazā…
Sung by Farida Khanum, Ghulam Ali and Pankaj Udhas

This is the ghazal containing the two lines Ghalib is said to have offered his entire divan for. Reading it whole shows what the excerpt cannot: fifteen different ways of arriving at the same two words, and a closing couplet that deliberately breaks the ambiguity the rest of the poem depends on.

1

اثر اس کو ذرا نہیں ہوتا
رنج راحت فزا نہیں ہوتا

asar us ko zarā nahīñ hotā
ranj rāhat-fazā nahīñ hotā

Nothing affects her in the slightest. And sorrow, it turns out, does not increase one's ease.

The matla — both lines carry the refrain

2

بے وفا کہنے کی شکایت ہے
تو بھی وعدہ وفا نہیں ہوتا

bevafā kahne kī shikāyat hai
to bhī vāda-vafā nahīñ hotā

She objects to being called faithless — and even so, not one promise is kept.

3

ذکر اغیار سے ہوا معلوم
حرف ناصح برا نہیں ہوتا

zikr-e-aġhyār se huā maʿlūm
harf-e-nāseh burā nahīñ hotā

Hearing her speak of my rivals taught me something: the adviser's words were not so bad after all.

The nāseh, the well-meaning counsellor, is normally the enemy

4

کس کو ہے ذوق تلخ کامی لیک
جنگ بن کچھ مزہ نہیں ہوتا

kis ko hai zauq-e-talḳh-kāmī lek
jang bin kuchh mazā nahīñ hotā

Who has any taste for bitterness? And yet without a quarrel there is no pleasure in it at all.

5

تم ہمارے کسی طرح نہ ہوئے
ورنہ دنیا میں کیا نہیں ہوتا

tum hamāre kisī tarah na hue
varna duniyā meñ kyā nahīñ hotā

By no means at all did you become mine — otherwise, what does not happen in this world?

6

اس نے کیا جانے کیا کیا لے کر
دل کسی کام کا نہیں ہوتا

us ne kyā jaane kyā kiyā le kar
dil kisī kaam kā nahīñ hotā

Who knows what she did with it once she had taken it — a heart is of no use to anyone.

7

امتحاں کیجیے مرا جب تک
شوق زور آزما نہیں ہوتا

imtihāñ kījiye mirā jab tak
shauq zor-āzmā nahīñ hotā

Put me to the test — while my longing is not yet strong enough to test its own strength.

8

ایک دشمن کہ چرخ ہے نہ رہے
تجھ سے یہ اے دعا نہیں ہوتا

ek dushman ki charḳh hai na rahe
tujh se ye ai duʿā nahīñ hotā

One enemy — the turning heavens — let it be gone. O prayer, even this you cannot manage.

9

آہ طول عمل ہے روز فزوں
گرچہ اک مدعا نہیں ہوتا

aah tūl-e-amal hai roz-fuzūñ
garche ik muddaʿā nahīñ hotā

Alas — my efforts lengthen day by day, though not one purpose of mine is achieved.

10

تم مرے پاس ہوتے ہو گویا
جب کوئی دوسرا نہیں ہوتا

tum mire paas hote ho goyā
jab koī dūsrā nahīñ hotā

You are, as it were, beside me — whenever no one else is.

The couplet Ghalib is said to have envied

11

حال دل یار کو لکھوں کیوں کر
ہاتھ دل سے جدا نہیں ہوتا

hāl-e-dil yaar ko likhūñ kyūñkar
hāth dil se judā nahīñ hotā

How am I to write my heart's condition to the beloved? My hand will not separate itself from my heart.

12

رحم کر خصم جان غیر نہ ہو
سب کا دل ایک سا نہیں ہوتا

rahm kar ḳhasm-e-jān-e-ġhair na ho
sab kā dil ek sā nahīñ hotā

Have mercy — do not become the enemy of another's life. Not everyone's heart is made the same.

13

دامن اس کا جو ہے دراز تو ہو
دست عاشق رسا نہیں ہوتا

dāman us kā jo hai darāz to ho
dast-e-āshiq rasā nahīñ hotā

Let her garment be as long as it likes. The lover's hand does not reach that far.

14

چارۂ دل سوائے صبر نہیں
سو تمہارے سوا نہیں ہوتا

chāra-e-dil sivā.e sabr nahīñ
so tumhāre sivā nahīñ hotā

There is no cure for the heart except patience — and that is not possible without you.

15

کیوں سنے عرض مضطر مومنؔ
صنم آخر خدا نہیں ہوتا

kyuuñ sune arz-e-muztar-e-'momin'
sanam āḳhir ḳhudā nahīñ hotā

Why should she hear Momin's desperate petition? An idol, after all, is not God.

The maqta · the pen name, and the ambiguity deliberately broken

What reading it whole shows. The ghazal spends fourteen couplets letting the beloved occupy the position that, in the Sufi reading, belongs to God — unmoved, unreachable, worth every humiliation. Then the last couplet names the difference outright: sanam is not ḳhudā. An idol is not God, so why would she answer a prayer? It is simultaneously a theological joke, a confession of idolatry, and the bitterest possible complaint — and it only works because of the fourteen couplets that set it up.

Muhammad Iqbal — Tarana-e-Hindi

Published in the weekly Ittehad, 16 August 1904 · collected in Bang-e-Dra (1924)
9 couplets, complete · Radif: hamārā

Written in ghazal form but functioning as a song, and composed for children. It is still sung across India — by the armed forces as a march, and in schools. Iqbal was 27, had not yet left for Cambridge, and would later argue for a separate Muslim state. Both facts are true, and the poem is a more complicated object for it.

1

سارے جہاں سے اچھا ہندوستاں ہمارا
ہم بلبلیں ہیں اس کی یہ گلستاں ہمارا

sāre jahāñ se achchhā hindostāñ hamārā
ham bulbuleñ haiñ is kī ye gulsitāñ hamārā

Better than all the world is our Hindustan. We are its nightingales; this is our garden.

The matla

2

غربت میں ہوں اگر ہم رہتا ہے دل وطن میں
سمجھو وہیں ہمیں بھی دل ہو جہاں ہمارا

ġhurbat meñ hoñ agar ham rahtā hai dil vatan meñ
samjho vahīñ hameñ bhī dil ho jahāñ hamārā

If we are far from home, the heart remains in the homeland. Consider us to be wherever our heart is.

3

پربت وہ سب سے اونچا ہمسایہ آسماں کا
وہ سنتری ہمارا وہ پاسباں ہمارا

parbat vo sab se ūñchā hamsāya āsmāñ kā
vo santarī hamārā vo pāsbāñ hamārā

That highest mountain, neighbour of the sky — that is our sentry, that is our watchman.

The Himalaya

4

گودی میں کھیلتی ہیں اس کی ہزاروں ندیاں
گلشن ہے جن کے دم سے رشک جناں ہمارا

godī meñ khelti haiñ is kī hazāroñ nadiyāñ
gulshan hai jin ke dam se rashk-e-janāñ hamārā

A thousand rivers play in its lap — by whose life our garden is the envy of paradise.

5

اے آب رود گنگا وہ دن ہیں یاد تجھ کو
اترا ترے کنارے جب کارواں ہمارا

ai āb-e-rūd-e-gangā vo din haiñ yaad tujh ko
utrā tire kināre jab kārvāñ hamārā

O waters of the Ganges, do you remember those days — when our caravan came down and halted on your bank?

6

مذہب نہیں سکھاتا آپس میں بیر رکھنا
ہندی ہیں ہم وطن ہے ہندوستاں ہمارا

mazhab nahīñ sikhātā āpas meñ bair rakhnā
hindī haiñ ham vatan hai hindostāñ hamārā

Religion does not teach us to hold enmity among ourselves. We are of Hind; our homeland is Hindustan.

The most quoted couplet in the poem

7

یونان و مصر و روما سب مٹ گئے جہاں سے
اب تک مگر ہے باقی نام و نشاں ہمارا

yūnān-o-misr-o-romā sab miṭ ga.e jahāñ se
ab tak magar hai bāqī nām-o-nishāñ hamārā

Greece, Egypt and Rome have all been erased from the world. Yet our name and trace remain to this day.

8

کچھ بات ہے کہ ہستی مٹتی نہیں ہماری
صدیوں رہا ہے دشمن دور زماں ہمارا

kuchh baat hai ki hastī miṭtī nahīñ hamārī
sadiyoñ rahā hai dushman daur-e-zamāñ hamārā

There is something in it, that our existence is never erased — though for centuries the turning of the age has been our enemy.

9

اقبال کوئی محرم اپنا نہیں جہاں میں
معلوم کیا کسی کو درد نہاں ہمارا

iqbāl koī mahram apnā nahīñ jahāñ meñ
maʿlūm kyā kisī ko dard-e-nihāñ hamārā

Iqbal, there is no confidant of ours anywhere in the world. What would anyone know of our hidden pain?

The maqta · a private turn after eight public couplets

The turn nobody quotes. Eight couplets of collective celebration — hamārā, ours, ours, ours — and then the ninth withdraws into complete isolation. The refrain that has meant "belonging to all of us" for eight couplets suddenly attaches to a pain no one shares. Iqbal ends his most communal poem alone, which is a formal decision, and an early sign of the preoccupation with the solitary self that becomes khudi.

Amir Khusrau — chhāp tilak sab chhīnī

Attributed to Amir Khusrau (1253–1325) · Hindavi / Braj, not Urdu
Sung as qawwali for seven centuries

Not a ghazal, and not in Urdu — this is Hindavi, the language Rekhta grew out of, in a woman's voice. The speaker addresses her pir, the Sufi master Nizamuddin Auliya, in the vocabulary of a bride. Human and divine love are not merely ambiguous here; they are the same sentence.

1

چھاپ تلک سب چھینی رے موسے نیناں ملائی کے

chhāp tilak sab chhīnī re mose naināñ milā.ike

You have taken everything from me — my mark, my ornament — just by meeting my eyes.

The refrain, returning after every line

2

پریم بھٹی کا مدوا پلائی کے
متوالی کر دینی رے موسے نیناں ملائی کے

prem bhaṭī kā madvā pilā.ike
matvālī kar dīnhī re mose naināñ milā.ike

Having made me drink the wine from love's still, you left me intoxicated — just by meeting my eyes.

3

گوری گوری بیّاں ہری ہری چوڑیاں
بیّاں پکڑ دھر لینی رے موسے نیناں ملائی کے

gorī gorī baiyyāñ harī harī chūṛiyāñ
baiyyāñ pakaṛ dhar līnhī re mose naināñ milā.ike

Fair, fair arms; green, green bangles — you seized my arms and held them, just by meeting my eyes.

The bangles are a bride's

4

بل بل جاؤں میں تورے رنگ ریجوا
اپنی سی کر دینی رے موسے نیناں ملائی کے

bal bal jāūñ maiñ tore rang-rejvā
apnī sī kar dīnhī re mose naināñ milā.ike

I would give myself over and over for you, my dyer — you dyed me your own colour, just by meeting my eyes.

The dyer is the master; the colour is his

5

خسرو نظام کے بل بل جائیے
موہے سہاگن کینی رے موسے نیناں ملائی کے

ḳhusrau nijām ke bal bal jaiye
mohe suhāgan kīnhī re mose naināñ milā.ike

Khusrau gives himself utterly to Nizam — he has made me a bride, just by meeting my eyes.

The signature couplet, naming both poet and master

On the attribution. A very large body of Hindavi verse circulates under Khusrau's name, and scholars agree that much of it accumulated over centuries of oral and qawwali transmission rather than being written by him. Khusrau's securely attributed work is overwhelmingly in Persian. This piece is traditional, beloved, and central to the qawwali repertoire — and its authorship, like most of the Hindavi corpus, cannot be established with the confidence that his Persian divans can. It is included because the tradition is unimaginable without it, with the doubt stated.
Why the modern poets appear only in extract. Everything reproduced in full on this page is out of copyright — Khusrau, Ghalib, Momin and Iqbal are all long past any term. Faiz, Faraz, Jaun Elia, Parveen Shakir, Nasir Kazmi, Habib Jalib and Munir Niazi are not: their work remains in copyright in Pakistan and India, and reproducing whole poems here would not be quotation but republication. They are quoted at couplet length, with attribution and commentary, which is what scholarly discussion allows. For their complete texts, the Rekhta archive carries the poems in Urdu, Devanagari and Roman side by side, and their collections remain in print.

The Lexicon: A Cast of Recurring Characters

The ghazal uses a fixed repertory of figures and images. They are not the poet's private symbols — they are shared property, and the artistry lies in what a poet does with an image everyone already knows.

Figure or imageLiterallyIn the poem
MehboobThe belovedGrammatically masculine by convention regardless of who is meant, and deliberately ambiguous between a human lover and God. Beautiful, indifferent, and usually cruel
Ishq-e-majazi / ishq-e-haqiqiMetaphorical / real loveThe organising distinction of the whole tradition: human love as the training ground for divine love. This is what licenses the ambiguity above — the reader is never meant to choose
Saqi, maikhana, sheeshaCup-bearer, tavern, wine-glassIntoxication as spiritual state. The tavern is where the honest are, as opposed to the mosque where the hypocrites are — a Sufi commonplace, not an endorsement of drinking
Zahid, naaseh, waizThe ascetic, the adviser, the preacherThe antagonists. Pious, literal-minded, and always wrong. Their function is to be answered
RaqeebThe rivalThe other lover. Sometimes envied, sometimes pitied as a fellow sufferer
Shama aur parwanaCandle and mothThe lover destroyed by approaching the beloved — and choosing it. The single most common image in the tradition
Gul o bulbulRose and nightingalePersian inheritance: the nightingale sings to a rose that cannot hear. Unrequited devotion as an ordering of the world
Qafas, sayyadCage, hunterConfinement. After 1857 and again after 1947, these images carry political weight the censor could not easily object to
Sahra, dashtDesert, wildernessWhere Majnun went mad for Laila. Madness as the proof of sincerity
Why the ambiguity is deliberate. Western readers often want to know whether a given ghazal is about a woman or about God. The question is usually the wrong one. The tradition constructed a vocabulary in which both readings remain live simultaneously, and the great couplets are precisely those that will not resolve. A poem that can only be read one way has failed at something the form is designed to do.

The Mushaira: Poetry as a Live Event

Urdu poetry was never primarily printed. It was performed, to an audience that talked back — and the form was shaped by that.

How it runs

Poets sit in a semicircle. A candle — the shama — is placed before whoever recites, and passed on, traditionally moving from the least to the most senior, so the evening builds.

The poet says arz kiya hai — "I have submitted" — and the audience answers irshād, "please proceed." The first line of a couplet is delivered, then repeated, sometimes several times, while the audience holds the rhyme scheme in mind and anticipates.

Then the second line lands. If it earns it, the room responds: wah wah, subhan Allah, mukarrar irshād — say it again. Poets routinely repeat a couplet three or four times on demand.

Why this shaped the poetry

The independence of the sher makes sense once you see the room. A couplet must work in isolation because it will be received in isolation, applauded, and repeated before the next one begins.

The radif makes sense too. A refrain the audience has already learned creates a shared expectation, and the poet's craft is measured by how surprisingly each couplet satisfies it.

Tarannum — reciting in melody rather than speech — is a distinct skill, and some poets are famous for it. Others deliver flat, on the argument that the words should not need help.

The tradition is fully alive: Jashn-e-Rekhta in Delhi draws crowds in the tens of thousands, and the online Rekhta archive has made hundreds of thousands of couplets searchable in three scripts.

The Modern Turn

Progressive Writers' Movement, 1936 · Partition, 1947

The classical lexicon of the beloved and the tavern was turned, almost intact, to politics — and turned out to be perfectly suited to writing under censorship.

The progressive movement

Founded in 1936, the Progressive Writers' Movement committed literature to anti-colonial and social concerns. Its central insight was formal rather than political: the ghazal's ambiguity, developed over centuries to hold human and divine love together, would just as readily hold a lover and a revolution together.

That is why so much of this poetry survived censorship. A vocabulary in which the beloved is never named, the wound is never specified and the morning is always still coming is extremely difficult to prosecute — and every reader in the room knows exactly what is meant.

The movement also split the tradition. Its critics argued that subordinating poetry to a programme cost it precision, and the halqa-e-arbab-e-zauq formed as a deliberate counterweight favouring craft over commitment. Both camps produced major work.

Partition, and after

1947 divided the language's territory, its readership and its institutions. Urdu became the national language of Pakistan and one of India's scheduled languages, and the same corpus began to be taught as two partly different literatures.

The literature of Partition is among the most unsparing writing on communal violence in any language — Saadat Hasan Manto's stories above all, of which Toba Tek Singh, set in a lunatic asylum whose inmates are to be divided by religion, is the one that has never lost its force.

In India, Firaq Gorakhpuri carried the classical line forward and won the Jnanpith for it, while Sahir Ludhianvi and Kaifi Azmi took progressive politics into Hindi cinema and reached audiences no book could. In Pakistan, the generations treated in the section above.

Agha Shahid Ali (1949–2001), Kashmiri and writing in English, brought the strict ghazal to American poetry and insisted it keep its rules rather than becoming a loose mood — the anthology Ravishing DisUnities is his argument.

A Timeline

c. 1700Wali Dakhni reaches DelhiProof that serious ghazal is possible in this language. The Delhi literati switch within a generation
1739Nadir Shah sacks DelhiThe disorder that shapes Mir's life and the theme of the ruined city that runs through the tradition
1723–1810Mir Taqi MirThe classical peak of plainness and feeling. Called khuda-e-sukhan, the god of poetry
1797–1869Mirza GhalibMetaphysical density in the ghazal; and a body of letters that creates modern Urdu prose
1857The uprising and its suppressionThe Mughal court abolished, Delhi's literary world destroyed. The classical age ends here
1803–1874Mir AnisThe marsiya raised to epic scale — the tradition's great narrative achievement
1877–1938Muhammad IqbalVerse as sustained philosophy; Shikwa, Jawab-e-Shikwa, the doctrine of khudi
1936Progressive Writers' MovementThe classical vocabulary redirected to politics, and the ghazal's ambiguity turned into a way of writing past censors
1947PartitionThe readership divided; the literature of displacement, from Manto to Faiz
1911–1984Faiz Ahmed FaizThe beloved and the revolution made grammatically inseparable. The most translated modern Urdu poet

2015–Jashn-e-RekhtaTens of thousands attending an annual Urdu festival; the online archive makes the corpus searchable across three scripts

If You Are Starting From Nothing

You do not need to learn the script to begin. Transliteration and a good translation will get you a long way, and the sound is available immediately.

A route in
  • Start with sung ghazals, not printed ones. Mehdi Hassan, Begum Akhtar, Farida Khanum, Jagjit Singh. The metre and the radif become obvious when you hear them, and you will start anticipating the rhyme before you understand the words.
  • Read one couplet at a time. Never a whole ghazal at first. The form does not require it and the density punishes speed.
  • Use a transliteration with diacritics. The Rekhta archive gives Urdu, Devanagari and Roman side by side, with a word-by-word dictionary.
  • Learn the lexicon above before the grammar. Twenty images unlock more poems than a hundred verb forms.
  • Then learn the script. Nastaliq is genuinely hard to read at first — it slopes, letters change shape by position, and short vowels are unwritten. It is also the most beautiful writing system in use anywhere, and it repays the month it takes.
On translation

Every translation on this page loses something specific, and it is worth naming what.

The metre goes. Quantitative Urdu prosody has no English equivalent, so the singability disappears entirely.

The radif goes. English word order will not let a refrain fall in the same place, so the anticipation the form is built on cannot be reproduced.

The ambiguity narrows. Urdu's grammar sustains multiple readings that English forces a translator to choose between — the Momin couplet above is the clearest case.

This is not an argument against translation. It is an argument for reading it beside the transliteration, and for saying the original aloud even without full comprehension. A surprising amount survives that route.

Ghalib expected to be remembered for his Persian and was wrong. Iqbal expected his philosophy to outlast his verse and was wrong. What survived in both cases was the couplet — two lines, complete in themselves, portable enough to be carried in conversation for two hundred years. That is what the form was built to do, and it still does it.
